Cloud Spanner.description:
GOOGLE CLOUD SPANNER

In This Page:

1. SpannerDeployInstanceOperato 2. SpannerDeleteInstanceOperato

3. SpannerDeployDatabaseInstanceOperator 4. SpannerUpdateDatabaseInstanceOperator

5. SpannerQueryDatabaseInstanceOperator 6. SpannerDeleteDatabaseInstanceOperator


1. SpannerDeployInstanceOperator

Creates a new Cloud Spanner instance, or if an instance with the same instance id exists in the specified project, updates the Cloud Spanner instance.

Parameters:

  • instance_id (str) â€“ Cloud Spanner instance ID.
  • configuration_name (str) â€“ The name of the Cloud Spanner instance configuration defining how the instance will be created. Required for instances that do not yet exist.
  • node_count (int) â€“ (Optional) The number of nodes allocated to the Cloud Spanner instance.
  • display_name (str) â€“ (Optional) The display name for the Cloud Spanner instance in the Google Cloud Console. (Must be between 4 and 30 characters.) If this value is not set in the constructor, the name is the same as the instance ID.
  • project_id (str) â€“ Optional, the ID of the project which owns the Cloud Spanner Database. If set to None or missing, the default project_id from the Google Cloud connection is used.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
  • impersonation_chain (str | collections.abc.Sequence[str] | None) â€“ Optional service account to impersonate using short-term credentials, or chained list of accounts required to get the access_token of the last account in the list, which will be impersonated in the request. If set as a string, the account must grant the originating account the Service Account Token Creator IAM role. If set as a sequence, the identities from the list must grant Service Account Token Creator IAM role to the directly preceding identity, with first account from the list granting this role to the originating account (templated).
# SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.spanner import SpannerDeployInstanceOperator

task = SpannerDeployInstanceOperator(
    project_id='your-project-id',
    instance_id='your-instance-id',
    configuration='regional-us-central1',
    node_count=1, # Or processing_units
    display_name='Instance Display Name',
    task_id='your_task_id'
)

# EXAMPLE
scale_spanner = SpannerDeployInstanceOperator(
    task_id="scale_up_for_load",
    instance_id="main-instance",
    configuration="projects/prod-project/instanceConfigs/regional-us-central1",
    node_count=3,
    display_name="Production Instance",
)


2. SpannerDeleteInstanceOperator

Permanently deletes an entire Spanner instance and all databases contained within it; if an instance does not exist, no action is taken and the task succeeds.

Parameters:

  • instance_id (str) â€“ The Cloud Spanner instance ID.
  • project_id (str) â€“ Optional, the ID of the project that owns the Cloud Spanner Database. If set to None or missing, the default project_id from the Google Cloud connection is used.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
  • impersonation_chain (str | collections.abc.Sequence[str] | None) â€“ Optional service account to impersonate using short-term credentials, or chained list of accounts required to get the access_token of the last account in the list, which will be impersonated in the request. If set as a string, the account must grant the originating account the Service Account Token Creator IAM role. If set as a sequence, the identities from the list must grant Service Account Token Creator IAM role to the directly preceding identity, with first account from the list granting this role to the originating account (templated).
# SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.spanner import SpannerDeleteInstanceOperator

task = SpannerDeleteInstanceOperator(
    project_id='your-project-id',
    instance_id='your-instance-id',
    task_id='your_task_id'
)

# EXAMPLE
teardown_env = SpannerDeleteInstanceOperator(
    task_id="delete_dev_instance",
    instance_id="dev-instance-123",
)



3. SpannerDeployDatabaseInstanceOperator

Creates a new Spanner database within an existing instance. It is idempotent; if the database already exists, the task succeeds without making changes.

Parameters:

  • instance_id (str) â€“ The Cloud Spanner instance ID.
  • database_id (str) â€“ The Cloud Spanner database ID.
  • ddl_statements (list[str]) â€“ The string list containing DDL for the new database.
  • project_id (str) â€“ Optional, the ID of the project that owns the Cloud Spanner Database. If set to None or missing, the default project_id from the Google Cloud connection is used.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
  • impersonation_chain (str | collections.abc.Sequence[str] | None) â€“ Optional service account to impersonate using short-term credentials, or chained list of accounts required to get the access_token of the last account in the list, which will be impersonated in the request. If set as a string, the account must grant the originating account the Service Account Token Creator IAM role. If set as a sequence, the identities from the list must grant Service Account Token Creator IAM role to the directly preceding identity, with first account from the list granting this role to the originating account (templated).
# SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.spanner import SpannerDeployDatabaseInstanceOperator

task = SpannerDeployDatabaseInstanceOperator(
    project_id='your-project-id',
    instance_id='your-instance-id',
    database_id='your-database-id',
    ddl_statements=['OPTIONAL_INITIAL_SCHEMA'],
    task_id='your_task_id'
)

# EXAMPLE
create_db = SpannerDeployDatabaseInstanceOperator(
    task_id="create_new_inventory_db",
    instance_id="main-instance",
    database_id="inventory_db",
    ddl_statements=[
        "CREATE TABLE Products (Id INT64 NOT NULL) PRIMARY KEY (Id)"
    ],
)


4. SpannerUpdateDatabaseInstanceOperator

You can optionally specify an operation_id parameter which simplifies determining whether the statements were executed in case the update_database call is replayed (idempotency check). The operation_id should be unique within the database, and must be a valid identifier: [a-z][a-z0-9_]*. 

Parameters:

  • instance_id (str) â€“ The Cloud Spanner instance ID.
  • database_id (str) â€“ The Cloud Spanner database ID.
  • ddl_statements (list[str]) â€“ The string list containing DDL to apply to the database.
  • project_id (str) â€“ Optional, the ID of the project that owns the Cloud Spanner Database. If set to None or missing, the default project_id from the Google Cloud connection is used.
  • operation_id (str | None) â€“ (Optional) Unique per database operation id that can be specified to implement idempotency check.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
  • impersonation_chain (str | collections.abc.Sequence[str] | None) â€“ Optional service account to impersonate using short-term credentials, or chained list of accounts required to get the access_token of the last account in the list, which will be impersonated in the request. If set as a string, the account must grant the originating account the Service Account Token Creator IAM role. If set as a sequence, the identities from the list must grant Service Account Token Creator IAM role to the directly preceding identity, with first account from the list granting this role to the originating account (templated).
# SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.spanner import SpannerUpdateDatabaseInstanceOperator

task = SpannerUpdateDatabaseInstanceOperator(
    project_id='your-project-id',
    instance_id='your-instance-id',
    database_id='your-database-id',
    ddl_statements=['LIST_OF_DDL_STRINGS'],
    task_id='your_task_id'
)

# EXAMPLE
update_schema = SpannerUpdateDatabaseInstanceOperator(
    task_id="add_phone_column",
    instance_id="main-instance",
    database_id="user_db",
    ddl_statements=[
        "ALTER TABLE Customers ADD COLUMN Phone STRING(32)"
    ],
)


5. SpannerQueryDatabaseInstanceOperator

Executes DML (Data Manipulation Language) statements, such as INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, and can also be used to run queries.

Parameters:

  • instance_id (str) â€“ The Cloud Spanner instance ID.
  • database_id (str) â€“ The Cloud Spanner database ID.
  • query (str | list[str]) â€“ The query or list of queries to be executed. Can be a path to a SQL file.
  • project_id (str) â€“ Optional, the ID of the project that owns the Cloud Spanner Database. If set to None or missing, the default project_id from the Google Cloud connection is used.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
  • impersonation_chain (str | collections.abc.Sequence[str] | None) â€“ Optional service account to impersonate using short-term credentials, or chained list of accounts required to get the access_token of the last account in the list, which will be impersonated in the request. If set as a string, the account must grant the originating account the Service Account Token Creator IAM role. If set as a sequence, the identities from the list must grant Service Account Token Creator IAM role to the directly preceding identity, with first account from the list granting this role to the originating account (templated).
# SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.spanner import SpannerQueryDatabaseInstanceOperator

task = SpannerQueryDatabaseInstanceOperator(
    project_id='your-project-id',
    instance_id='your-instance-id',
    database_id='your-database-id',
    query='SQL_QUERY_OR_PATH_TO_SQL_FILE',
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default',
    task_id='your_task_id'
)

# EXAMPLE
execute_dml = SpannerQueryDatabaseInstanceOperator(
    task_id="insert_customer_record",
    project_id="prod-analytics",
    instance_id="main-instance",
    database_id="user_db",
    query="INSERT INTO Customers (ID, Name) VALUES (101, 'Acme Corp')",
)


6. SpannerDeleteDatabaseInstanceOperator

Deletes a database from the specified Cloud Spanner instance. If the database does not exist, no action is taken, and the operator succeeds.

Parameters:

  • instance_id (str) â€“ Cloud Spanner instance ID.
  • database_id (str) â€“ Cloud Spanner database ID.
  • project_id (str) â€“ Optional, the ID of the project that owns the Cloud Spanner Database. If set to None or missing, the default project_id from the Google Cloud connection is used.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
  • impersonation_chain (str | collections.abc.Sequence[str] | None) â€“ Optional service account to impersonate using short-term credentials, or chained list of accounts required to get the access_token of the last account in the list, which will be impersonated in the request. If set as a string, the account must grant the originating account the Service Account Token Creator IAM role. If set as a sequence, the identities from the list must grant Service Account Token Creator IAM role to the directly preceding identity, with first account from the list granting this role to the originating account (templated).
# SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.spanner import SpannerDeleteDatabaseInstanceOperator

task = SpannerDeleteDatabaseInstanceOperator(
    project_id='your-project-id',
    instance_id='your-instance-id',
    database_id='your-database-id',
    task_id='your_task_id'
)

# EXAMPLE
cleanup_db = SpannerDeleteDatabaseInstanceOperator(
    task_id="delete_temp_db",
    instance_id="main-instance",
    database_id="temp_staging_db",
)

Cloud Storage.description:
GOOGLE CLOUD STORAGE

Here's the list formatted in the same style:

1. GCSCreateBucketOperator

2. GCSListObjectsOperator

3. GCSDeleteObjectsOperator

4. GCSFileTransformOperator

5. GCSTimeSpanFileTransformOperator

6. GCSDeleteBucketOperator

7. GCSSynchronizeBucketsOperator

8. GCSObjectExistenceSensor

9. GCSObjectUpdateSensor

10. GCSObjectsWithPrefixExistenceSensor

ï»¿11. GCSUploadSessionCompleteSensor


1. GCSCreateBucketOperator

Creates a new Google Cloud Storage bucket with specified configuration options. This operator is used when you need to programmatically create storage buckets as part of your data pipeline initialization or setup workflows.

Parameters:

  • bucket_name (str) â€“ The name of the bucket. (templated)
  • resource (dict | None) â€“ An optional dict with parameters for creating the bucket. For information on available parameters, see Cloud Storage API doc: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/json_api/v1/buckets/insert
  • storage_class (str) â€“ MULTI_REGIONAL, REGIONAL, STANDARD, NEARLINE, COLDLINE, If this value is not specified when the bucket is created, it will default to STANDARD.
  • location (str) â€“ The location of the bucket. (templated) Object data for objects in the bucket resides in physical storage within this region. Defaults to US.
  • project_id (str) â€“ The ID of the Google Cloud Project. (templated)
  • labels (dict | None) â€“ User-provided labels, in key/value pairs.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ (Optional) The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.gcs import GCSCreateBucketOperator
create_bucket = GCSCreateBucketOperator(
    task_id='create_bucket',
    bucket_name='my-bucket-name',
    project_id='my-project-id',
    storage_class='STANDARD',
    location='US'
)

#EXAMPLE
create_data_lake_bucket = GCSCreateBucketOperator(
    task_id='create_data_lake_bucket',
    bucket_name='company-data-lake-{{ ds_nodash }}',
    project_id='analytics-project-12345',
    storage_class='STANDARD',
    location='us-central1',
    labels={
        'environment': 'production',
        'department': 'analytics',
        'created_by': 'airflow'
    },
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


2. GCSListObjectsOperator

Lists all objects in a Google Cloud Storage bucket that match specified criteria. This operator is useful for discovering files in GCS buckets, validating data availability, or dynamically generating task dependencies based on available files.

Parameters:

  • bucket (str) â€“ The Google Cloud Storage bucket to find the objects. (templated)
  • prefix (str | list[str] | None) â€“ String or list of strings, which filter objects whose name begins with it/them. (templated)
  • delimiter (str | None) â€“ (Deprecated) The delimiter by which you want to filter the objects. (templated) For example, to list the CSV files from in a directory in GCS you would use delimiter=â€™.csvâ€™.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ (Optional) The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
  • match_glob (str | None) â€“ (Optional) filters objects based on the glob pattern given by the string (e.g, '**/*.json')
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.gcs import GCSListObjectsOperator
list_objects = GCSListObjectsOperator(
    task_id='list_objects',
    bucket='my-bucket',
    prefix='data/',
    match_glob='**/*.csv'
)

#EXAMPLE
list_daily_reports = GCSListObjectsOperator(
    task_id='list_daily_reports',
    bucket='sales-reports-bucket',
    prefix='reports/2024/01/',
    match_glob='**/*_sales_report.csv',
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


3. GCSDeleteObjectsOperator

Deletes objects from a Google Cloud Storage bucket. This operator is essential for cleanup tasks, managing storage costs by removing obsolete data, or implementing data retention policies in your pipelines.

Parameters:

  • bucket_name (str) â€“ The GCS bucket to delete from
  • objects (list[str] | None) â€“ List of objects to delete. These should be the names of objects in the bucket, not including gs://bucket/
  • prefix (str | list[str] | None) â€“ String or list of strings, which filter objects whose name begin with it/them. (templated)
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ (Optional) The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.gcs import GCSDeleteObjectsOperator
delete_objects = GCSDeleteObjectsOperator(
    task_id='delete_objects',
    bucket_name='my-bucket',
    objects=['file1.txt', 'file2.csv']
)

#EXAMPLE
cleanup_old_logs = GCSDeleteObjectsOperator(
    task_id='cleanup_old_logs',
    bucket_name='application-logs-bucket',
    prefix='logs/2023/',
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)

delete_temp_files = GCSDeleteObjectsOperator(
    task_id='delete_temp_files',
    bucket_name='processing-bucket',
    objects=[
        'temp/intermediate_data_{{ ds }}.csv',
        'temp/validation_results_{{ ds }}.json'
    ]
)


4. GCSFileTransformOperator

Transforms files from a source GCS bucket and uploads the results to a destination GCS bucket. This operator downloads files, applies a transformation function, and uploads the transformed output, making it ideal for data preprocessing, format conversions, or data enrichment tasks. if destination path is not mentioned, it will overwrite the source.

Parameters:

  • source_bucket (str) â€“ The bucket to locate the source_object. (templated)
  • source_object (str) â€“ The key to be retrieved from GCS. (templated)
  • destination_bucket (str | None) â€“ The bucket to upload the key after transformation. If not provided, source_bucket will be used. (templated)
  • destination_object (str | None) â€“ The key to be written in GCS. If not provided, source_object will be used. (templated)
  • transform_script (str | list[str]) â€“ location of the executable transformation script or list of arguments passed to subprocess ex. [â€˜pythonâ€™, â€˜script.pyâ€™, 10]. (templated)
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID to use connecting to Google Cloud.
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.gcs import GCSFileTransformOperator

transform_file = GCSFileTransformOperator(
    task_id='transform_file',
    source_bucket='source-bucket',
    source_object='input.csv',
    destination_bucket='dest-bucket',
    destination_object='output.csv',
    transform_script=['python', '/path/to/transform.py']
)

#EXAMPLES
convert_csv_to_json = GCSFileTransformOperator(
    task_id='convert_csv_to_json',
    source_bucket='raw-data-bucket',
    source_object='sales/daily_sales_{{ ds }}.csv',
    destination_bucket='processed-data-bucket',
    destination_object='sales/daily_sales_{{ ds }}.json',
    transform_script=['python', '/usr/local/airflow/scripts/csv_to_json.py'],
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


5. GCSTimeSpanFileTransformOperator

Transforms files within a specified time range from a source GCS bucket to a destination bucket. This operator is particularly useful for batch processing time-series data where you need to transform multiple files created within a specific time window.

Parameters:

  • source_bucket (str) â€“ The bucket to fetch data from. (templated)
  • source_prefix (str) â€“ Prefix string which filters objects whose name begin with this prefix. Can interpolate logical date and time components. (templated)
  • source_gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID to use connecting to Google Cloud to download files to be processed.
  • destination_bucket (str) â€“ The bucket to write data to. (templated)
  • destination_prefix (str) â€“ Prefix string for the upload location. Can interpolate logical date and time components. (templated)
  • destination_gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID to use connecting to Google Cloud to upload processed files.
  • transform_script (str | list[str]) â€“ location of the executable transformation script or list of arguments passed to subprocess ex. [â€˜pythonâ€™, â€˜script.pyâ€™, 10]. (templated)
  • chunk_size (int | None) â€“ The size of a chunk of data when downloading or uploading (in bytes). This must be a multiple of 256 KB (per the google clout storage API specification).
  • download_continue_on_fail (bool | None) â€“ With this set to true, if a download fails the task does not error out but will still continue.
  • upload_chunk_size â€“ The size of a chunk of data when uploading (in bytes). This must be a multiple of 256 KB (per the google clout storage API specification).
  • upload_continue_on_fail (bool | None) â€“ With this set to true, if an upload fails the task does not error out but will still continue.
  • upload_num_attempts (int) â€“ Number of attempts to try to upload a single file.
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.gcs import GCSTimeSpanFileTransformOperator

transform_timespan_files = GCSTimeSpanFileTransformOperator(
    task_id='transform_timespan_files',
    source_bucket='source-bucket',
    source_prefix='logs/',
    destination_bucket='processed-bucket',
    destination_prefix='processed-logs/',
    transform_script=['python', '/path/to/script.py']
)

#EXAMPLE
process_hourly_logs = GCSTimeSpanFileTransformOperator(
    task_id='process_hourly_logs',
    source_bucket='raw-logs-bucket',
    source_prefix='application/logs/{{ ds }/',
    destination_bucket='analytics-bucket',
    destination_prefix='processed/logs/{{ ds }}/',
    transform_script=['python', '/opt/airflow/scripts/aggregate_logs.py'],
    source_object_required=False,
    source_gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default',
    destination_gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


6. GCSDeleteBucketOperator

Deletes a Google Cloud Storage bucket. This operator is used for cleaning up temporary buckets, removing unused resources, or implementing automated resource lifecycle management in your data pipelines.

Parameters:

  • bucket_name (str) â€“ name of the bucket which will be deleted
  • force (bool) â€“ false not allow to delete non empty bucket, set force=True allows to delete non empty bucket
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID to use connecting to Google Cloud.
  • user_project (str | None) â€“ (Optional) The identifier of the project to bill for this request. Required for Requester Pays buckets.
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.gcs import GCSDeleteBucketOperator

delete_bucket = GCSDeleteBucketOperator(
    task_id='delete_bucket',
    bucket_name='temporary-bucket',
    force=True
)

#EXAMPLE
cleanup_temp_bucket = GCSDeleteBucketOperator(
    task_id='cleanup_temp_bucket',
    bucket_name='temp-processing-bucket-{{ ds_nodash }}',
    force=True,
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


7. GCSSynchronizeBucketsOperator

Synchronizes objects between two Google Cloud Storage buckets. This operator copies new or updated files from a source bucket to a destination bucket, making it perfect for backup operations, data replication, or multi-region data distribution.

Parameters:

  • source_bucket (str) â€“ The name of the bucket containing the source objects.
  • destination_bucket (str) â€“ The name of the bucket containing the destination objects.
  • source_object (str | None) â€“ The root sync directory in the source bucket.
  • destination_object (str | None) â€“ The root sync directory in the destination bucket.
  • recursive (bool) â€“ If True, subdirectories will be considered
  • allow_overwrite (bool) â€“ if True, the files will be overwritten if a mismatched file is found. By default, overwriting files is not allowed
  • delete_extra_files (bool) â€“
  • if True, deletes additional files from the source that not found in the destination. By default extra files are not deleted.
  • Note
  • This option can delete data quickly if you specify the wrong source/destination combination.
  • gcp_conn_id (str) â€“ (Optional) The connection ID used to connect to Google Cloud.
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.gcs import GCSSynchronizeBucketsOperator

sync_buckets = GCSSynchronizeBucketsOperator(
    task_id='sync_buckets',
    source_bucket='source-bucket',
    destination_bucket='destination-bucket',
    recursive=True
)

#EXAMPLE
backup_production_data = GCSSynchronizeBucketsOperator(
    task_id='backup_production_data',
    source_bucket='production-data-us-central1',
    destination_bucket='backup-data-us-east1',
    source_object='critical/databases/',
    destination_object='backups/{{ ds }}/',
    recursive=True,
    allow_overwrite=True,
    delete_extra_files=False,
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


8. GCSObjectExistenceSensor

Checks for the existence of a specific object in a Google Cloud Storage bucket. This sensor waits until the specified file exists before allowing downstream tasks to proceed, making it essential for implementing dependencies on external file arrivals or ensuring data availability.

Parameters:

  • bucket (str) â€“ The Google Cloud Storage bucket where the object is.
  • object (str) â€“ The name of the object to check in the Google cloud storage bucket.
  • use_glob (bool) â€“ When set to True the object parameter is interpreted as glob
  • google_cloud_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID to use when connecting to Google Cloud Storage.
  • retry (google.api_core.retry.Retry) â€“ (Optional) How to retry the RPC
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.sensors.gcs import GCSObjectExistenceSensor

wait_for_file = GCSObjectExistenceSensor(
    task_id='wait_for_file',
    bucket='my-bucket',
    object='data/input.csv'
)

#EXAMPLE
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.sensors.gcs import GCSObjectExistenceSensor

wait_for_daily_extract = GCSObjectExistenceSensor(
    task_id='wait_for_daily_extract',
    bucket='external-vendor-bucket',
    object='exports/customer_data_{{ ds }}.csv',
    poke_interval=300,
    timeout=3600,
    mode='poke',
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


9. GCSObjectUpdateSensor

Monitors a Google Cloud Storage object and waits until it has been updated after a specified timestamp. This sensor is useful for detecting when files have been refreshed or modified, ensuring your pipeline processes the latest version of data.

Parameters:

  • bucket (str) â€“ The Google Cloud Storage bucket where the object is.
  • object (str) â€“ The name of the object to download in the Google cloud storage bucket.
  • ts_func (collections.abc.Callable) â€“ Callback for defining the update condition. The default callback returns logical_date + schedule_interval. The callback takes the context as parameter.
  • google_cloud_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID to use when connecting to Google Cloud Storage.
  • deferrable (bool) â€“ Run sensor in deferrable mode
#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.sensors.gcs import GCSObjectUpdateSensor

wait_for_update = GCSObjectUpdateSensor(
    task_id='wait_for_update',
    bucket='my-bucket',
    object='data/master_file.csv'
)

#EXAMPLE
from airflow.utils.dates import days_ago

wait_for_config_update = GCSObjectUpdateSensor(
    task_id='wait_for_config_update',
    bucket='configuration-bucket',
    object='settings/application_config.json',
    ts_func=lambda: days_ago(1),
    poke_interval=120,
    timeout=7200,
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


10. GCSObjectsWithPrefixExistenceSensor

Checks for the existence of objects matching a specified prefix in a Google Cloud Storage bucket. This sensor is valuable for waiting on multiple files or ensuring a minimum number of files exist before processing, commonly used for batch processing scenarios.

Parameters:

  • bucket (str) â€“ The Google Cloud Storage bucket where the object is.
  • prefix (str) â€“ The name of the prefix to check in the Google cloud storage bucket.
  • google_cloud_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID to use when connecting to Google Cloud Storage.
  • deferrable (bool) â€“ Run sensor in deferrable mode
#SYNTAX

from airflow.providers.google.cloud.sensors.gcs import GCSObjectsWithPrefixExistenceSensor

wait_for_files = GCSObjectsWithPrefixExistenceSensor(
    task_id='wait_for_files',
    bucket='my-bucket',
    prefix='data/input/'
)

#EXAMPLE
wait_for_daily_partitions = GCSObjectsWithPrefixExistenceSensor(
    task_id='wait_for_daily_partitions',
    bucket='data-warehouse-bucket',
    prefix='raw/transactions/{{ ds }}/',
    min_objects=24,  # Wait for all 24 hourly files
    poke_interval=600,
    timeout=86400,
    mode='reschedule',
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)


11. GCSUploadSessionCompleteSensor

Waits for all expected objects in an upload session to be present in a Google Cloud Storage bucket. This sensor is designed for scenarios where multiple files are being uploaded concurrently, and you need to ensure the entire batch is complete before proceeding with processing.

Parameters:

  • bucket (str) â€“ The Google Cloud Storage bucket where the objects are. expected.
  • prefix (str) â€“ The name of the prefix to check in the Google cloud storage bucket.
  • inactivity_period (float) â€“ The total seconds of inactivity to designate an upload session is over. Note, this mechanism is not real time and this operator may not return until a poke_interval after this period has passed with no additional objects sensed.
  • min_objects (int) â€“ The minimum number of objects needed for upload session to be considered valid.
  • previous_objects (set[str] | None) â€“ The set of object ids found during the last poke.
  • allow_delete (bool) â€“ Should this sensor consider objects being deleted between pokes valid behavior. If true a warning message will be logged when this happens. If false an error will be raised.
  • google_cloud_conn_id (str) â€“ The connection ID to use when connecting to Google Cloud Storage.
  • deferrable (bool) â€“ Run sensor in deferrable mode


#SYNTAX
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.sensors.gcs import GCSUploadSessionCompleteSensor

wait_for_upload_complete = GCSUploadSessionCompleteSensor(
    task_id='wait_for_upload_complete',
    bucket='upload-bucket',
    prefix='session/2024-01-01/',
    inactivity_period=300,
    min_objects=10
)

#EXAMPLE
wait_for_batch_upload = GCSUploadSessionCompleteSensor(
    task_id='wait_for_batch_upload',
    bucket='incoming-data-bucket',
    prefix='uploads/partner_feed_{{ ds }}/',
    inactivity_period=600,  # 10 minutes of no new files
    min_objects=50,  # Expect at least 50 files
    allow_delete=False,
    poke_interval=180,
    timeout=14400,  # 4 hours timeout
    mode='reschedule',
    gcp_conn_id='google_cloud_default'
)

1. DataFrame.__getattr__(name): Column

Enables dynamic attribute access on a DataFrame, typically used in PySpark to access column names as attributes (e.g., `df.column_name`).

Tip: Avoid overriding this for normal attribute access to prevent masking methods or existing attributes; use it primarily for syntactic sugar column access.

2. DataFrame.__getitem__(item): Column | DataFrame

Used for column selection or subsetting by label or boolean array, often acting as the indexing operator (e.g., `df['col']` or `df[[bool_array]]`). Tip: Favor explicit column selection over row slicing to maintain Spark's distributed nature and avoid costly data movements.

df[['first_name', 'age']].show(2)
df['first_name'].show(2)

3. DataFrame.select(*cols):DataFrame

Projects a set of expressions (columns) to return a new DataFrame, essentially defining a subset or derived view of the original data. Tip: Use `selectExpr` for simpler expression-based column transformations when you need to define new columns on the fly.

df.select("first_name", "age", "salary").show(3)

It allows projecting new or existing columns using SQL expressions for flexible transformations, which is great for leveraging existing SQL knowledge or complex column manipulations. A key tip is to always prefer standard DataFrame API operations over SQL expressions in selectExpr for better performance and type safety unless the SQL syntax offers a significant advantage.


df.selectExpr("first_name", "age", "salary * 0.1 as bonus").show(3)

â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”


DataFrame.join(other[, on, how]):DataFrame

Combines columns of two or more DataFrames by merging them based on index or specified key columns, similar to SQL joins.

Tips: Ensure both sides of the join use the same data types for join keys, apply filtering early, and use broadcast joins only for small, static DataFrames to avoid out-of-memory errors.


DataFrame.lateralJoin(other[, on, how]):DataFrame

`DataFrame.lateralJoin` applies a Table-Valued Function (TVF) to each row of the left DataFrame, enabling the right DataFrame to dynamically reference columns from that current row for context-dependent expansion.


DataFrame.crossJoin(other):DataFrame

Returns the cartesian product, matching every row in the left DataFrame with every row in the right DataFrame. Be cautious using this method on large DataFrames as it can lead to performance issues due to the exponential growth in rows.


DataFrame.unionAll(other):DataFrame

Combines two DataFrames row-wise, preserving all rows including duplicates, but note that `unionAll()` is deprecated since Spark 2.0.0; use `union()` instead, which also preserves duplicates by default when used without the `distinct` operation.


DataFrame.unionByName(other[, ...]):DataFrame

Combines rows from two DataFrames by matching column names instead of position, simplifying unions when schemas differ in column order. Use the allowMissingColumns=True parameter if you need to union DataFrames with different sets of columns, as it will fill in missing columns with NULL values.


DataFrame.intersect(other):DataFrame

Returns a new DataFrame containing only the distinct rows that exist in both DataFrames. Tip: Use `intersectAll()` if you need to preserve duplicate rows in the intersection.


DataFrame.intersectAll(other):DataFrame

DataFrame.intersectAll finds the common rows between two DataFrames, crucially preserving all duplicates, which is equivalent to SQL's INTERSECT ALL. Tip: Remember it resolves columns by position, not by name.


DataFrame.exceptAll(other):DataFrame

Returns a new DataFrame containing rows in the source DataFrame but not in the compared DataFrame, preserving all duplicates, acting as the SQL EXCEPT ALL operation. Tip: Columns are resolved by position, not by name, which is critical for consistent results.


DataFrame.subtract(other):DataFrame

Used to subtract elements of another DataFrame or Series from the calling DataFrame, aligning data by both index and column. Tip: Be mindful of NaN generation when indexes don't align perfectly.

5.Grouping & Aggregation

â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”

DataFrame.groupBy(*cols):pandas.api.typing.DataFrameGroupBy

The primary purpose of the groupby method is to split a DataFrame into groups based on some criterion, apply a function (like aggregation, transformation, or filtration) to each group, and then combine the results. Tip: Use as_index=False when performing aggregations if you want the grouping column(s) to remain as data columns rather than becoming the index of the resulting DataFrame.


DataFrame.agg(*exprs): scalar, Series, or DataFrame

It's used to apply one or more aggregation functions across a DataFrame, typically after a `groupBy` operation, to summarize data. Tip: Use named aggregation (e.g., column.alias) for clarity when applying multiple aggregations to specific columns.



DataFrame.rollup(*cols):DataFrame

The DataFrame.rollup method is used for hierarchical aggregation, creating multi-dimensional summaries that include all specified column combinations, subtotals, and a grand total for multi-dimensional analysis and reporting. Tip: Use with the agg function to apply multiple aggregation metrics efficiently across all rollup levels.


DataFrame.cube(*cols):DataFrame

Creates multi-dimensional aggregations (like an OLAP cube) across specified columns, generating results for all possible subtotal combinations, including a grand total. Tip: Be mindful of performance, as the number of combinations grows exponentially with the number of columns used in the cube operation.


DataFrame.groupingSets(groupingSets, *cols):GroupedData

It enables multi-dimensional aggregation across specified subsets of grouping columns, producing results equivalent to a union of multiple GROUP BY clauses. Tip: For common hierarchical summaries, prefer using the more optimized .rollup() or .cube() methods, as `groupingSets` is more general and can sometimes be less performant if not carefully implemented.


DataFrame.crosstab(col1, col2):DataFrame

Computes a contingency table (pair-wise frequency) between two specified columns for data exploration and relationship analysis; ensure the columns selected are categorical or have a manageable number of distinct values to avoid extremely wide tables.


DataFrame.unpivot(ids, values, ...):DataFrame

It transforms a wide DataFrame into a long format, which is the reverse of a pivot operation; ensure all value columns share a least common data type and use an ID column if you need to retain identifying information.


DataFrame.melt(ids, values, ...):DataFrame

Unpivots a DataFrame from a "wide" format to a "long" format by turning columns into rows for easier analysis; ensure you clearly define your identifier and measured variables.

6.Sorting & Ordering:

DataFrame.orderBy(*cols, **kwargs):DataFrame

Used to return a new DataFrame sorted by the specified column(s); tip: use `orderBy()` when the order is critical, as it guarantees the output data is ordered.


DataFrame.sort(*cols, **kwargs):DataFrame or None

Sorts the DataFrame by values in specified columns or by the index, enabling ordered data retrieval and analysis. Tip: For large datasets, always consider using `sort_values()` with the `inplace=False` default to ensure performance and avoid unexpected side effects, and be mindful of memory usage if sorting triggers data shuffling across partitions.


DataFrame.sortWithinPartitions(*cols, **kwargs):DataFrame

Sorts rows within each partition of a DataFrame locally without triggering a global shuffle, optimizing for performance when global ordering is not required. Tip: Use this method in conjunction with `repartition` or `partitionBy` when generating partitioned files (e.g., Parquet) to ensure each resulting file is internally sorted.

7.Column Operations

â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”

DataFrame.withColumn(colName, col):DataFrame

The DataFrame.withColumn method returns a new DataFrame by adding a new column or replacing an existing column with the same name, based on a given Column expression. Tip: Avoid using this method repeatedly in loops for adding multiple columns, as it generates large execution plans and can cause performance degradation; use `select()` or `withColumns()` instead.


DataFrame.withColumns(*colsMap):DataFrame

DataFrame.withColumns adds or replaces multiple columns in a DataFrame in a single efficient transformation by accepting a dictionary of column names and expressions. Tip: Always prefer using withColumns over calling withColumn repeatedly in a loop when adding many columns to avoid performance bottlenecks and complex logical plans.


DataFrame.withColumnRenamed(existing, new):Returns a new DataFrame with the renamed column.

Returns a new DataFrame by renaming an existing column without modifying the existing DataFrame or schema. Tip: For renaming multiple columns, chain multiple calls or consider using `toDF` with a sequence of new column names if the order is guaranteed and all columns are being renamed.


DataFrame.withColumnsRenamed(colsMap):DataFrame

Returns a new DataFrame by renaming multiple columns simultaneously using a dictionary mapping of old to new column names. Tip: Since Spark 3.4.0, this method supports renaming multiple columns, whereas `withColumnRenamed` only supports one at a time.


DataFrame.withMetadata(columnName, metadata):DataFrame

DataFrame.withMetadata enables attaching crucial context and documentation (metadata) to a DataFrame or its columns, essential for data lineage and consumption clarity.


DataFrame.drop(*cols):DataFrame or None

The DataFrame.drop() method returns a new DataFrame with specified columns removed, or specified labels removed from columns or index in the case of pandas-on-Spark. A key tip is to be mindful of ambiguous column references when dropping columns after a join, as this can lead to errors.

8.Transformation & Mapping

â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”

DataFrame.transform(func, *args, **kwargs):DataFrame or Series

DataFrame transformations create a new DataFrame or RDD from an existing one, enabling data manipulation and processing; ensure efficient execution by understanding the difference between narrow and wide transformations to minimize costly data shuffling.


DataFrame.mapInPandas(func, schema[, ...]):DataFrame

It enables applying a Python function that uses pandas DataFrames to each partition of a Spark DataFrame, bridging distributed processing with Python's data manipulation capabilities.

Tip: Ensure your function expects and returns an iterator of pandas DataFrames, and be mindful of data serialization overhead between Spark and Python processes.


DataFrame.mapInArrow(func, schema[, ...]):DataFrame

DataFrame.mapInArrow efficiently applies a custom Python function to DataFrame partitions using PyArrow for high-throughput data exchange.

Tip: Always define explicit input/output schemas for improved performance and error handling.


DataFrame.foreach(f):void

Applies a function to all rows of the DataFrame, typically used for side-effect operations like updating accumulators or writing to external data sources. Tip: Since execution is distributed, be mindful of resource consumption and state management within the function applied to each row.


DataFrame.foreachPartition(f):void

Executes a specified function for each partition of the DataFrame, primarily used for efficiency when performing heavy initialization tasks like opening database connections once per partition. Tip: Leverage it for operations requiring costly setup, such as writing to external data sources (RDBMS, Kafka), to minimize initialization overhead.

9.Missing Data Handling

â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”

DataFrame.fillna(value[, subset]):Series/DataFrame

Used to impute missing or null values (NaN) within a DataFrame with a specified value or method. Be mindful that applying fillna() across the entire DataFrame without specifying columns will fill all NaN values, potentially causing unintended data modification.


DataFrame.dropna([how, thresh, subset]):DataFrame or None

DataFrame.dropna removes rows or columns containing missing values (NaN or None) from your DataFrame; Tip: Always verify the 'axis' parameter (0 for rows, 1 for columns) and consider 'thresh' to avoid losing too much data.


DataFrame.na:boolean same-sized object

DataFrame.na provides access to functionality for handling missing or null/NaN values within a Spark DataFrame, allowing operations like dropping or filling these values.

Tip: Always ensure you understand the difference between dropping rows with 'any' versus 'all' nulls when using drop().


DataFrameNaFunctions.drop([how, thresh, subset]):DataFrame

Removes rows from a DataFrame that contain null or NaN values based on specified criteria (any/all nulls, minimum non-null threshold, and optional subset of columns). Tip: Always specify the subset of columns if you only want to check for nulls within those columns, rather than the entire DataFrame.


DataFrameNaFunctions.fill(value[, subset]):DataFrame

The purpose of `pyspark.sql.DataFrameNaFunctions.fill()` is to replace null values within a DataFrame with a specified replacement value or a mapping of column-specific values. Tip: Be mindful of data types; the replacement value must match or be compatible with the column's data type, otherwise the column will be ignored.


DataFrameNaFunctions.replace(to_replace[, ...]):DataFrame

The `DataFrameNaFunctions.replace` method is used to return a new DataFrame by replacing specified values with other values across all or a subset of columns. Tip: Ensure `to_replace` and `value` types match the column data types, which must be numerics, booleans, or strings.

10.Statistical Functions:

â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”

DataFrame.corr(col1, col2[, method]):DataFrame

Calculates the Pearson correlation coefficient between two specified columns in a DataFrame, and note that it currently only supports the Pearson method.


DataFrame.cov(col1, col2):DataFrame

DataFrame.cov calculates the sample covariance for a pair of specified columns; ensure data types are numeric or the operation will fail silently, ignoring non-numeric columns.


DataFrame.freqItems(cols[, support]):DataFrame

This method computes frequent items in specified DataFrame columns, useful for identifying popular values in the dataset. A key tip is to be mindful that this function is primarily for exploratory data analysis and doesn't guarantee backward compatibility of the resulting schema.


DataFrame.approxQuantile(col, probabilities, ...):list

DataFrame.approxQuantile efficiently approximates quantiles for numerical columns in large datasets, balancing accuracy and performance. Remember to manage the relative error parameter (relativeError) to control the trade-off between accuracy and computation time, especially for very large data.


DataFrame.stat:DataFrameStatFunctions

Provides access to a collection of statistical functions like correlation, covariance, and quantiles for a Spark DataFrame. Tip: Leverage DataFrameStatFunctions for efficient, distributed statistical computations instead of rolling your own RDD-based logic.


DataFrameStatFunctions.approxQuantile(col, ...):list

Calculates the approximate quantiles for one or multiple numerical columns in a DataFrame, which is useful for large datasets where exact quantile calculation is computationally expensive. Tip: Carefully choose the relative error to balance between accuracy and performance; a smaller error means higher accuracy but longer computation time.


DataFrameStatFunctions.corr(col1, col2[, method]):float

Calculates the correlation coefficient (currently limited to Pearson) between two specified columns in a DataFrame; ensure both columns are numeric or casting will be necessary.


DataFrameStatFunctions.cov(col1, col2):float or None (depending on the implementation and data)

Calculates the sample covariance between two numerical columns of a DataFrame to measure how they vary together. Tip: Ensure both columns are of a numerical data type for the calculation to succeed.


DataFrameStatFunctions.crosstab(col1, col2):DataFrame

Computes a pair-wise frequency table (contingency table) for two specified columns, showing the frequency matrix between their distinct values. Tip: Be aware that for columns with a large number of distinct values, the resulting contingency table can be very wide and consume significant memory.


DataFrameStatFunctions.freqItems(cols[, support]):DataFrame

Used to efficiently compute frequent items across specified columns in a DataFrame, which is useful for preliminary data analysis and discovering common occurrences. *Tip: Be aware this is an approximate algorithm that may yield false positives, and its schema is not guaranteed to be backward compatible.*


DataFrameStatFunctions.sampleBy(col, fractions):DataFrame

Performs stratified sampling without replacement based on specified fractions for different strata defined by a column. Tip: Always ensure your fractions dictionary covers all desired strata, as unlisted ones default to a zero fraction.

11.Materialization & Actions

â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”


DataFrame.collect():List of Row objects

The primary purpose of `DataFrame.collect()` is to materialize the entire distributed dataset from the cluster executors onto the driver node as a local list of Row objects, and a critical tip is to only use it when the resulting dataset is small enough to fit comfortably within the driver's available memory.


DataFrame.count():int (pyspark) or Series/DataFrame (pandas)

DataFrame.count() is used to synchronously return the total number of rows in the DataFrame. Tip: This method triggers a full job execution, so use it sparingly on large datasets for performance optimization.


DataFrame.take(num):DataFrame or Series

Returns the first *num* rows of a DataFrame as a list of Row objects; avoid using `take()` on very large datasets as it can move a significant amount of data to the driver node.


DataFrame.toLocalIterator([prefetchPartitions]):iterator (of Row objects)

DataFrame.toLocalIterator is used to iterate through DataFrame rows locally on the driver node without loading the entire dataset into memory, which is essential for processing massive datasets efficiently. Be cautious, as the iterator will consume memory equal to the largest partition, potentially causing OutOfMemory errors on the driver if partitions are too large.


DataFrame.exists():Column

Checks for the existence of related rows in a subquery, returning a boolean column. Tip: Use caution with performance on very large DataFrames as this can involve shuffling or broadcasting.

12.Partitioning & Performance

â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”â€”

DataFrame.repartition(numPartitions, *cols):DataFrame

The DataFrame.repartition method redistributes the data across a specified number of partitions, typically for workload balancing, optimizing joins, or preparing for write operations. Use it judiciously as it involves a costly full shuffle of data across the network; prioritize coalesce for decreasing partitions.


DataFrame.repartitionByRange(numPartitions, ...):DataFrame

It repartitions a DataFrame by range based on specified column expressions, which is key for optimizing query performance by ensuring data locality. Tip: Always specify at least one partition-by expression.


DataFrame.coalesce(numPartitions):DataFrame

Used to reduce the number of partitions in a DataFrame to a specified number without a full shuffle, which is generally faster than repartition when decreasing partitions, but can lead to data skew if not careful.


DataFrame.cache():Table

Persists the DataFrame in memory for significantly faster subsequent operations and iterative algorithms; always assign the cached DataFrame to a new variable (`cached_df = original_df.cache()`) to ensure the cache is used, and only cache medium-sized, frequently accessed datasets.


DataFrame.persist([storageLevel]):New dask collections backed by in-memory data (Dask) or DataFrame (PySpark)

The primary purpose of `DataFrame.persist` is to materialize a DataFrame, storing its contents across operations to avoid repeated computation, making subsequent actions faster; ensure you choose the appropriate `StorageLevel` to balance memory usage and fault tolerance.


DataFrame.unpersist([blocking]):DataFrame

DataFrame.unpersist marks the DataFrame as non-persistent, removing its cached data from memory and disk to free up resources. Tip: Use unpersist(blocking=True) to guarantee the operation completes before proceeding, especially in interactive environments.


DataFrame.checkpoint([eager]):DataFrame

It truncates the logical plan of a DataFrame to prevent exponential growth in iterative algorithms by saving the state to disk, which is especially useful when the execution plan becomes complex; ensure a checkpoint directory is set with SparkContext.setCheckpointDir() before use.


DataFrame.localCheckpoint([eager, storageLevel]):DataFrame

Truncates the DataFrame's logical plan to prevent exponential growth, which is critical for iterative algorithms, but remember that local checkpoints are stored in the executors' cache and are thus unreliable and will be lost if the executor fails.


DataFrame.storageLevel:str

It specifies how and where a Spark DataFrame is persisted or cached, dictating its availability and fault tolerance. Tip: Use `MEMORY_ONLY_SER` for memory efficiency if re-computation is fast, and always remember to `unpersist()` when the DataFrame is no longer needed to free up resources.


DataFrame.hint(name, *parameters):DataFrame

Specifies optimization hints to the Spark query optimizer to influence query execution plans for potential performance improvement; tip: use hints judiciously and only after performance analysis, as incorrect hints can sometimes degrade performance.

DataFrame.toPandas():pandas.DataFrame

Converts a distributed Spark DataFrame into a local, in-memory Pandas DataFrame. Tip: Only use this method when the resulting Pandas DataFrame is small, as all data is loaded into the driver's memory.


DataFrame.toJSON([use_unicode]):For pandas.DataFrame.to_json: string or None.

For pyspark.sql.DataFrame.toJSON: RDD of string.

This method efficiently converts a Spark DataFrame into an RDD of JSON strings, where each row becomes a JSON document. Tip: Be aware that `toJSON()` returns an RDD of strings, not another DataFrame, which is crucial for subsequent operations like saving or collecting data.

toDF


DataFrame.toArrow():Table

The DataFrame.toArrow method converts a Spark DataFrame into a PyArrow Table for efficient interoperability, but use it only on small datasets because all data is collected into the driver's memory.


DataFrame.toDF(*cols):DataFrame

The `DataFrame.toDF(*cols)` method is used to return a new DataFrame with the specified column names, which is particularly useful for renaming columns or converting an RDD with default column names (like _1, _2) into a structured DataFrame. Tip: Ensure the number of new column names provided matches the number of columns in the original DataFrame or RDD.


DataFrame.to(schema):Series

The `toPandas()` method converts a Spark DataFrame into a Pandas DataFrame, pulling all distributed data into the driver's memory. This method should only be used when the resulting Pandas DataFrame is expected to be small, as all data is loaded into the driver program's memory.


DataFrame.transpose([indexColumn]):DataFrame

The purpose of the `DataFrame.transpose` method in PySpark is to pivot the DataFrame, making values from a specified index column the new column headers.

Tip: Ensure all non-index columns share a least common data type before transposing.


DataFrame.pandas_api([index_col]):DataFrame

The pandas_api is designed to provide compatibility and a standardized set of methods for DataFrame operations across different Python data analysis libraries, ensuring code portability. When utilizing this API, be mindful that the underlying implementation may differ from native pandas, potentially affecting performance characteristics and lazy evaluation behaviors in distributed or out-of-core systems.


DataFrame.asTable():TableArg object

The `DataFrame.asTable()` method converts a DataFrame into a `TableArg` object, enabling its use as a table argument in Table-Valued Functions (TVFs) like UDTFs. Tip: Be aware that `withSinglePartition` cannot be called after `partitionBy()` has been used.

DataFrame.write(:The return type for DataFrame.write is not specified in the provided context or search results.

DataFrame.write provides the interface for saving the contents of a DataFrame to various external storage systems or tables.


Tips: * Always specify the appropriate write mode (e.g., "overwrite", "append") to handle existing data correctly.

* Leverage `partitionBy()` for better query performance and to manage output file size, using `coalesce()` to reduce partitions when writing output to avoid small file issues.

DataFrame.writeStream:DataStreamWriter

DataFrame.writeTo(table):DataFrameWriter

The DataFrame.writeTo method is used to persist the contents of a DataFrame to various external data sources, specifying the target and handling modes for existing data. Always define the desired write mode (e.g., append, overwrite) to prevent accidental data loss or duplication.

15.Views & Tables

DataFrame.createTempView(name):None

It creates a temporary, session-scoped view of the DataFrame allowing it to be queried using Spark SQL. Tip: Remember that temporary views are tied to the SparkSession and will disappear when the session ends.


DataFrame.createOrReplaceTempView(name):List[Row]

This method registers the DataFrame as a lazily-evaluated, temporary, session-scoped SQL view, allowing it to be queried using Spark SQL.

Tip: Remember that temporary views are session-scoped and are dropped when the SparkSession terminates, so they cannot be shared across sessions or persist across application runs.


DataFrame.createGlobalTempView(name):None

DataFrame.createGlobalTempView registers the DataFrame as a view accessible across all Spark sessions throughout the application's lifetime under the "global_temp" namespace. Tip: Always access these views using the "global_temp." prefix in your SQL queries (e.g., SELECT * FROM global_temp.view_name).


DataFrame.createOrReplaceGlobalTempView(name):None

Creates or replaces a temporary view that is shared across all Spark sessions within the application, lasting for the application's lifetime; use this when you need to query the data from different sessions or notebooks.


DataFrame.registerTempTable(name):None

DataFrame.explain([extended, mode]):string

The `DataFrame.explain()` method is used for debugging and optimization by printing the logical and physical execution plans of a DataFrame to the console. Tip: Always examine the physical plan to identify potential data shuffles or suboptimal joins.


DataFrame.inputFiles():list

Returns a list of input file paths that were read to constitute the DataFrame, providing transparency on the data's source. Tip: This method is primarily reliable for file-based sources (like Parquet or CSV) and may return an empty list for database sources (like JDBC).


DataFrame.isEmpty():bool

pyspark.sql.DataFrame.isEmpty efficiently checks if a DataFrame has any rows, returning a boolean without triggering a full computation; use it over `count() == 0` for performance and remember it's available from Spark 3.3.0 onwards.


DataFrame.isLocal():boolean

The `DataFrame.isLocal()` method checks if the data operations like `collect()` and `take()` can be executed entirely on the driver without involving Spark executors; use this primarily for small DataFrames to avoid unnecessary distributed execution overhead.


DataFrame.isStreaming:bool

This property checks if a DataFrame is sourced from continuous data streams, returning True for streaming DataFrames and False otherwise. Tip: Always check isStreaming before attempting to use a streaming sink (like .writeStream) or a batch operation.


DataFrame.executionInfo:ExecutionInfo object

Returns an ExecutionInfo object after a DataFrame query has been executed, providing details necessary for monitoring and analyzing the physical plan. Always use this to inspect the actual execution plan and look for data skew or costly shuffles to optimize your jobs.


DataFrame.sparkSession:SparkSession

It returns the underlying SparkSession associated with the DataFrame, which is the primary entry point for all Spark functionality, and a key tip is to always use the existing SparkSession builder pattern to avoid resource conflicts.


DataFrame.semanticHash():integer

`DataFrame.semanticHash()` computes a hash code to efficiently determine if two DataFrames have the identical schema structure (column names and data types).

Tip: It's important to remember this hash is based on the schema/structure, not the data contents.


DataFrame.sameSemantics(other):bool

The DataFrame.sameSemantics method is used to quickly compare two DataFrames to determine if their underlying logical query plans are equal, which implies they should return the same results. Tip: This comparison is very fast but can sometimes return False even when DataFrames produce the same results due to different plans (a false negative).

DataFrame.withWatermark(eventTime, ...):DataFrame

Defines an event time watermark on a streaming DataFrame to manage late-arriving data and minimize state for aggregations and joins; always define watermarks on event-time columns, not ingestion time.



DataFrame.observe(observation, *exprs):DataFrame

It's used to define and compute named metrics/aggregates on the DataFrame execution path for monitoring and debugging performance. DataFrame.randomSplit(weights[, seed]):List[DataFrame]

Used to randomly split a DataFrame into multiple new DataFrames based on specified weights. Tip: Always set a seed for reproducibility across runs.


DataFrame.replace(to_replace[, value, subset]):Series/DataFrame

The `DataFrame.replace` method is used for substituting existing values within a DataFrame column or across the entire DataFrame with new specified values.

Tip: When replacing multiple values using sequences for `to_replace` and `value`, ensure they are of the same length and type.


DataFrame.scalar():object

DataFrame.scalar() is used to extract a Column object representing a single scalar value from a DataFrame, typically from an aggregation or single-value computation, for use in other queries or filters. DataFrame.summary(*statistics):Series or DataFrame

DataFrame.mergeInto(table, condition):MergeIntoWriter

DataFrame.alias(alias): DataFrame

The `DataFrame.alias` method is used to assign a shorter, more meaningful alias to a DataFrame, significantly improving code readability and simplifying complex joins, especially when dealing with column name conflicts. SparkSession.description:
pyspark.sql.SparkSession


SparkSession was introduced in version Spark 2.0, it is an entry point to underlying Spark functionality in order to programmatically create Spark RDD, DataFrame, and DataSet. It consolidates several previously separate contexts, such as SQLContext, HiveContext, and StreamingContext, into one entry point, to simplify the interaction to spark and APIs


Methods:

1. pyspark.sql.SparkSession.active(): SparkSession

ï»¿Returns the active or default SparkSession for the current thread, returned by the builder.

spark = SparkSession.active()  # Output: <pyspark.sql.session.SparkSession object at 0x7f8b3c4d5e10>

2. pyspark.sql.SparkSession.builder.appName(name:str): SparkSession.Builder

Apache Spark.description:
Apache Spark


Apache Spark is a unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing. It provides high-level APIs in Java, Scala, Python and R, and an optimized engine that supports general execution graphs. It also supports a rich set of higher-level tools including 


Components of Spark:

1. Spark Core:

Spark Core is the "engine room" of the entire Spark ecosystem. While libraries like Spark SQL or MLlib provide the user-friendly tools, Spark Core is what actually moves the data, manages the memory, and recovers from crashes.

Think of Spark Core as the operating system of the cluster. Its responsibilities are divided into four main pillars:

A. The RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset)

The RDD is the most fundamental component of Spark Core. It is the core data abstraction that makes everything else possible.

  • Resilient: If a part of the data is lost (e.g., a server crashes), Spark Core knows how to rebuild it.
  • Distributed: The data is chopped into "partitions" and spread across many machines.
  • Dataset: It is simply a collection of records (like a list or a table).

How "Resilience" works: Lineage

Instead of duplicating data across many disks (which is slow), Spark Core tracks the Lineage of the data. It remembers the "recipe" used to create the current dataset.

Example: If you had a list of names, filtered for names starting with "A," and then converted them to uppercaseâ€”and a machine failsâ€”Spark Core just looks at the recipe and reruns those two steps on the missing piece of data.


B. Infrastructure & Resource Management

Spark Core acts as the bridge between your code and the hardware.

  • Task Scheduling: It breaks your application into small "tasks" and decides which worker node should run which task. It prioritizes Data Locality (running the code on the machine that already holds the data to avoid moving it over the network).
  • Memory Management: This is Spark's "secret sauce." Spark Core manages the Unified Memory Manager, which balances memory between:
  • Execution Memory: Used for shuffles, joins, and sorts.
  • Storage Memory: Used for caching and "persisting" data you want to reuse.
  • Fault Recovery: It monitors the health of the executors. If an executor dies, Spark Core detects it and automatically moves its work to a healthy node.


C. The DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)

Every time you perform an operation in Spark, Spark Core doesn't run it immediately. Instead, it builds a DAGâ€”a logical map of every step in your process.

  • Directed: There is a clear flow from start to finish.
  • Acyclic: There are no loops (it won't get stuck in a circle).
  • Graph: A structure of nodes (data) and edges (operations).

By building this graph first, Spark Core can look at the whole plan and optimize it (e.g., merging two "filter" steps into one) before touching any data. This is part of Lazy Evaluation.


D. Networking and I/O

Spark Core handles the "dirty work" of moving data around.

  • Shuffling: This is the most expensive part of big data. If you need to group data by "City," Spark Core has to physically move all records for "London" to one machine and "New York" to another. This is called a Shuffle, and Spark Core manages the complex network logic to make this happen.
  • External Storage: Spark Core provides the basic I/O functions to read and write data from HDFS, Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, or local files.



2. Spark SQL:

Spark SQL is the most widely used component of the Spark ecosystem. It provides a programming abstraction called DataFrames and acts as a distributed SQL query engine.

While Spark Core works with raw, unstructured objects (RDDs), Spark SQL understands the structure of your data. This "awareness" allows Spark to optimize your code automatically, often making it much faster than manual Spark Core code.

A. Key Concepts: DataFrames and Datasets

Spark SQL moves away from the low-level RDDs to more structured abstractions:

  • DataFrame: Essentially a table spread across a cluster. It has named columns and a schema (e.g., "ID" is an integer, "Name" is a string). It is conceptually similar to a table in a relational database or a dataframe in Python's Pandas.
  • Dataset: A type-safe version of DataFrames available in Scala and Java. It provides the best of both worlds: the optimization of Spark SQL and the compile-time error checking of RDDs.


B. The Catalyst Optimizer (The Brains)

The most powerful part of Spark SQL is the Catalyst Optimizer. When you write a SQL query or a DataFrame operation, Catalyst transforms your code into an optimized physical execution plan.

It goes through four main phases:

  1. Analysis: It checks the names of columns and tables against a "Catalog" to make sure they exist.
  2. Logical Optimization: It applies rule-based optimizations. For example, if you filter data after a join, Catalyst will "push down" the filter so it happens before the join, reducing the amount of data moved.
  3. Physical Planning: It generates multiple ways the cluster could actually execute the task (e.g., choosing between a "SortMergeJoin" or a "BroadcastHashJoin") and picks the cheapest one based on a cost model.
  4. Code Generation: It generates Java bytecode to run on each machine, making the execution as fast as hand-written code.


C. Project Tungsten (The Muscle)

If Catalyst is the "brain," Tungsten is the "muscle." It focuses on improving the efficiency of Spark's memory and CPU usage:

  • Off-Heap Memory Management: It manages memory manually instead of relying on the Java Garbage Collector (GC), which prevents "stop-the-world" pauses in large applications.
  • Binary Processing: It stores data in a compact binary format rather than as heavy Java objects, fitting much more data into RAM.


E. Connectivity: The Thrift Server

Spark SQL isn't just for programmers. It includes a Thrift JDBC/ODBC Server. This allows business analysts to connect BI tools like Tableau, PowerBI, or Looker directly to Spark. They can run standard SQL queries against massive datasets, and Spark SQL will handle the distributed processing in the background.


3. Spark Streaming:

Enables scalable, high-throughput, fault-tolerant stream processing of live data streams (like Twitter feeds or IoT sensor data).


4. MLlib (Machine Learning Library):

A library of common machine learning algorithms (classification, regression, clustering, etc.) designed to scale across a cluster.


5. GraphX:

A library for manipulating graphs (like social networks or web links) and performing graph-parallel computation.

QueryBasics.description:
BigQuery MERGE Statement

MERGE is a single SQL statement that can INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE rows in a target table based on conditions from a source table. It's like a smart sync operation.

#--------------------------| SYNTAX |---------------------#
MERGE target_table AS T
USING source_table AS S
ON T.key_column = S.key_column

-- When row exists in BOTH target and source
WHEN MATCHED [AND condition] THEN
  UPDATE SET T.col1 = S.col1, T.col2 = S.col2
  -- OR
  DELETE

-- When row exists in source but NOT in target
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET [AND condition] THEN
  INSERT (col1, col2, col3)
  VALUES (S.col1, S.col2, S.col3)

-- When row exists in target but NOT in source
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE [AND condition] THEN
  UPDATE SET T.status = 'inactive'
  -- OR
  DELETE

#--------------------------| EXAMPLE |---------------------#
MERGE `project.dataset.employees` AS T
USING `project.dataset.hr_system_updates` AS S
ON T.employee_id = S.employee_id

-- CASE 1: Employee exists in both tables (MATCHED)
-- Update their information
WHEN MATCHED AND S.is_active = TRUE THEN
  UPDATE SET 
    T.name = S.name,
    T.department = S.department,
    T.salary = S.salary,
    T.status = 'active',
    T.last_updated = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()

-- CASE 2: Employee exists in both, but marked for termination
-- Delete them from our system
WHEN MATCHED AND S.is_active = FALSE THEN
  DELETE

-- CASE 3: Employee exists in HR system but NOT in our database
-- Insert new employee (NOT MATCHED BY TARGET)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
  INSERT (employee_id, name, department, salary, status, created_at, last_updated)
  VALUES (
    S.employee_id, 
    S.name, 
    S.department, 
    S.salary, 
    'active',
    CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(),
    CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
  )

-- CASE 4: Employee exists in our database but NOT in HR system
-- Mark as inactive (NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND T.status = 'active' THEN
  UPDATE SET 
    T.status = 'inactive',
    T.deactivated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()

Breaking Down the Example

Setup Tables

Target Table: employees

employee_id | name      | department | salary | status
------------|-----------|------------|--------|--------
1           | Alice     | IT         | 80000  | active
2           | Bob       | HR         | 70000  | active
3           | Charlie   | Sales      | 65000  | active

Source Table: hr_system_updates

employee_id | name      | department | salary | is_active
------------|-----------|------------|--------|----------
1           | Alice     | Engineering| 85000  | TRUE      (updated dept & salary)
2           | Bob       | HR         | 70000  | FALSE     (terminated)
4           | Diana     | Marketing  | 75000  | TRUE      (new employee)

What Happens After MERGE

Result in employees table:

employee_id | name      | department  | salary | status
------------|-----------|-------------|--------|----------
1           | Alice     | Engineering | 85000  | active     (UPDATED)
3           | Charlie   | Sales       | 65000  | inactive   (marked inactive)
4           | Diana     | Marketing   | 75000  | active     (INSERTED)

Note: Bob (employee_id=2) was DELETED

Understanding Each Clause

1. WHEN MATCHED

  • Condition: Row with same key exists in BOTH tables
  • Actions: UPDATE or DELETE the target table
  • Example: Alice exists in both â†’ update her info

2. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET

  • Condition: Row exists in SOURCE but NOT in TARGET
  • Actions: INSERT into target table
  • Example: Diana is new in HR system â†’ insert her

3. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE

  • Condition: Row exists in TARGET but NOT in SOURCE
  • Actions: UPDATE or DELETE from target table
  • Example: Charlie not in HR updates â†’ mark inactive

Key Concepts

Target Table: The table being modified (all changes happen here) Source Table: The table providing data (never modified, just read) ON Clause: Defines how to match rows between tables (usually primary key) Multiple Conditions: You can have multiple WHEN clauses with different conditions

Common Patterns

1. Simple Upsert (Insert or Update)

MERGE products AS T
USING product_updates AS S
ON T.product_id = S.product_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET T.price = S.price
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
  INSERT (product_id, price) VALUES (S.product_id, S.price)

2. Full Sync (Insert, Update, Delete)

MERGE inventory AS T
USING warehouse_data AS S
ON T.sku = S.sku
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET T.quantity = S.quantity
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
  INSERT (sku, quantity) VALUES (S.sku, S.quantity)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN
  DELETE

3. Conditional Operations

MERGE orders AS T
USING order_updates AS S
ON T.order_id = S.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND S.status = 'cancelled' THEN
  DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND S.total > T.total THEN
  UPDATE SET T.total = S.total, T.updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET AND S.status != 'cancelled' THEN
  INSERT (order_id, total, status) VALUES (S.order_id, S.total, S.status)

Important Rules

  1. Each source row can match at most one target row
  2. All operations happen on the target table only
  3. You can have multiple WHEN clauses with different conditions
  4. Clauses are evaluated in order (first match wins)
  5. BY TARGET can be omitted (it's the default for NOT MATCHED)
