Dataset.description:
Dataset

Datasets are top-level containers that are used to organize and control access to your tables and views. A table or view must belong to a dataset, so you need to create at least one dataset before loading data into BigQuery. 

Here are all 5 dataset type sections rewritten in a consistent, clean format:

1. Standard Datasets (Native)

The default and most powerful dataset type in BigQuery. Data is stored in BigQuery's proprietary Capacitor (columnar) format on Google's Colossus distributed file system. All BigQuery-native features are fully supported, making this the go-to choice for production workloads.

Hybrid Hub: Acts as a parent container â€” while it primarily hosts native tables, it can also contain Views, Materialized Views, and External/BigLake table definitions all within a single dataset.

Performance Optimization: Fully supports Clustering, Partitioning, Search Indexes, and Vector Search, enabling high-performance analytics and AI/ML workloads.

Storage Tiers: Automatically transitions table data from Active to Long-term storage after 90 consecutive days without modification â€” reducing storage costs by ~50% with no impact on query performance or accessibility.

Billing Models: Logical â€” billed on uncompressed data size (default) - Physical â€” billed on compressed, on-disk size; cost-effective for highly compressible data

Notes:

  • Only dataset type that supports Clustering, Partitioning, Search Indexes, Vector Search, Time Travel, and Fail-safe.
  • The 90-day Long-term storage timer resets if the table is modified (e.g., data inserted, schema changed).
  • Physical billing saves cost only when data compresses well; always evaluate before switching.
  • Supports both table-level and dataset-level expiration policies.
  • Default choice unless you have a specific reason to use External, Hidden, or Linked datasets.


2. External Datasets (Federated)

A metadata layer that acts as a direct window to data residing outside of BigQuery storage. Unlike standard datasets where you define individual external tables one by one, an External Dataset links an entire external database (e.g., Spanner, Cloud SQL, Bigtable) at the dataset level â€” all its tables become automatically accessible in BigQuery.

Dataset-Level Connection: A single connection to an external system exposes all its tables inside BigQuery, eliminating the need to define each table individually.

Zero-ETL: Data is queried directly in place â€” no ingestion or movement required. Any changes in the source system (e.g., a new row in Spanner) are immediately visible in BigQuery.

BigLake Integration: External tables can be upgraded to BigLake tables, enabling fine-grained Row/Column level security on files stored in GCS, S3, or Azure Blob Storage â€” just like native tables.

Notes:

  • No support for Time Travel, Fail-safe, or Table Expiration.
  • Read-only â€” DML operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) are not supported through BigQuery.
  • Performance is slower than native tables due to network latency and lack of physical data optimization.
  • BigLake upgrade is the recommended path when security enforcement on external files is needed.
  • Best used when data must stay in the source system but needs to be queryable from BigQuery.
  • Acts as a metadata pointer â€” no data is physically stored in BigQuery.


3. Authorized Datasets

A security-focused design pattern that grants a Consumer dataset permission to query tables in a Source (Shared) dataset. Any view created inside the Consumer dataset can access Source data â€” even if the end user running the query has no direct IAM access to the Source dataset itself.

How It Works: Instead of authorizing each view individually, you authorize the entire Consumer dataset once. All views within it automatically inherit access to the Source dataset.

Scalability: Ideal for multi-tenant architectures â€” authorize 1 dataset instead of managing permissions for 100+ individual views.

Implementation Flow:

  1. Export shared dataset metadata: bq show --format=prettyjson PROJECT:SHARED_DS > ds_meta.json
  2. Add the authorized Consumer dataset ID to the access array in the JSON.
  3. Apply the update: bq update --source ds_meta.json PROJECT:SHARED_DS

Notes:

  • The authorization is set on the Source dataset, not the Consumer dataset.
  • End users only need access to the Consumer dataset's views â€” not the Source tables.
  • External tables are supported as source, but end users must have IAM permissions on the underlying data source (e.g., storage.objects.get for GCS).
  • Hidden datasets cannot be used as the Source for an Authorized Dataset.
  • Best practice for sharing sensitive data without exposing raw tables to end users.


4. Hidden Datasets

A special dataset type identified by a leading underscore in the name (e.g., _staging_ds). Designed for internal tool staging, background processing, and temporary workloads that should not be visible or discoverable by general users or catalog tools.

Visibility: Completely invisible in the Cloud Console Explorer and excluded from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SCHEMATA â€” they do not surface in standard dataset listings.

Strict Isolation:

  • No Sharing â€” Cannot be used as a Source for Authorized Views or Authorized Datasets.
  • No Cataloging â€” Excluded from Dataplex and Data Catalog indexing.
  • No Linking â€” Cannot be used with Linked Datasets (Analytics Hub cross-project/cross-org sharing).

Discovery: The only way to list hidden datasets is via the CLI with the all flag: bq ls -a

Notes:

  • Naming is the key â€” any dataset whose name starts with _ is automatically treated as hidden.
  • Useful for staging intermediate data in pipelines without polluting the data catalog.
  • Despite being hidden from the UI, standard IAM permissions still apply â€” access is not automatically restricted.
  • Cannot participate in any cross-dataset sharing or governance workflows.
  • Not suitable for datasets that need to be shared, governed, or linked externally.


5. Linked Datasets (Analytics Hub)

The modern standard for cross-project and cross-organization data sharing in BigQuery. A Linked Dataset is a read-only reference created via Analytics Hub, pointing to a dataset shared (published) by another project or organization â€” without physically copying or moving the data.

Cross-Project Sharing: Data publishers list datasets on Analytics Hub as Listings. Subscribers create a Linked Dataset in their own project, which acts as a live pointer to the publisher's data.

Automatic Sync: Any metadata changes in the source (e.g., new columns added, schema updates) automatically propagate to all Linked Datasets â€” no manual refresh needed.

Billing Model:

  • Publisher pays for storage of the source data.
  • Subscriber pays for the query compute when querying the linked dataset.

Notes:

  • Linked Datasets are always read-only â€” subscribers cannot modify source data.
  • Metadata changes sync automatically, but data access is always live â€” there is no local copy in the subscriber's project.
  • Cannot be used as a Source for Authorized Datasets.
  • Best suited for sharing large, stable datasets (e.g., public data, partner data exchanges) without duplication costs.

Requires Analytics Hub to be enabled in both the publisher and subscriber projects.


CRUD OPERATIONS

IAM permission needed to create a dataset bigquery.datasets.create.

Each of the following predefined IAM roles includes the permissions that you need in order to create a dataset:

roles/bigquery.dataEditor roles/bigquery.dataOwner roles/bigquery.user roles/bigquery.admin


Notes:

The user wants to enhance the Notes section in their documentation page. This is a text editing/content task, not a document creation task. I'll craft well-organized, crisp notes segregated by section.

Here are the enhanced Notes sections, organized under each relevant topic:

Create

-- Requires bigquery.datasets.create IAM permission.

-- --max_time_travel_hours must be a multiple of 24 (e.g., 48, 72 ... 168).

-- In the Client Library, dataset.location must be set before calling create_dataset().


Update

-- update_dataset() in the Client Library requires explicitly passing the list of fields to update â€” unlisted fields are ignored.

-- storage_billing_model can be switched between PHYSICAL and LOGICAL at any time, but billing changes take effect immediately.


Delete

-- SQL DROP SCHEMA only deletes empty datasets by default; use CASCADE to delete all contents.

-- CLI bq rm -r -f -d skips confirmation prompt â€” use with caution in automation.

-- Client Library: delete_contents=True mirrors CASCADE; not_found_ok=True prevents errors on already-deleted datasets.


Copy Dataset

-- Uses BigQuery Data Transfer Service under the hood â€” not a native bq cp.

-- data_source is always cross_region_copy, even for same-region copies.

-- Only one transfer run is active at a time; additional runs are queued.

-- Minimum interval between copy jobs: 12 hours.

-- The following are not copied: Views, UDFs/Routines, External tables, CDC tables.

-- If the source table is unchanged, it is skipped. If changed, the destination table is fully truncated and replaced (no append support).

-- Cross-region copy with CMEK requires the destination dataset to also be encrypted with a matching CMEK.


Time Travel

-- Default window: 7 days. Configurable from 2 to 7 days (set in multiples of 24 hours).

-- Applies to: querying deleted/updated data, restoring deleted tables/datasets, and reverting to a prior state.

-- Set at the dataset or project level â€” applies to all tables within.

-- A shorter window reduces storage costs only when using the Physical billing model; no savings with Logical billing.

-- Time travel is not supported on External datasets.


Time Travel Restore

-- The snapshot timestamp in CLI (--snapshot_time) is in milliseconds (Unix epoch).

-- SQL restore creates a new table â€” the original name must be explicitly provided in FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF.

-- Restore is only possible within the configured time travel window (default 7 days).


List Datasets

-- INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SCHEMATA does not show hidden datasets (those with a leading _).

-- Use bq ls -a (CLI) to include hidden datasets.

-- Client Library's list_datasets() returns DatasetListItem objects â€” use .dataset_id for the ID only (does not include the full project path by default).



___________________________________________________________________________________________
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>| 'CREATE' |<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<

.......................................| 'SQL' |...........................................
CREATE SCHEMA PROJECT_ID.DATASET_ID
  OPTIONS (
    default_kms_key_name = 'KMS_KEY_NAME',
    default_partition_expiration_days = PARTITION_EXPIRATION,
    default_table_expiration_days = TABLE_EXPIRATION,
    description = 'DESCRIPTION',
    labels = [('KEY_1','VALUE_1'),('KEY_2','VALUE_2')],
    location = 'LOCATION',
    max_time_travel_hours = HOURS,
    storage_billing_model = BILLING_MODEL);

.......................................| 'CLI' |...........................................
# Initialize a new dataset in a specific region
bq mk --location=LOCATION \
      --dataset \
      --default_kms_key=KMS_KEY_NAME \                      # Set default encryption key for all new tables
      --default_partition_expiration=PARTITION_EXPIRATION \ # Set default partition TTL (seconds)
      --default_table_expiration=TABLE_EXPIRATION \         # Set default table TTL (seconds)
      --description="DESCRIPTION" \                         # Add dataset metadata description
      --label=KEY_1:VALUE_1 \                               # Assign metadata labels (Key:Value)
      --label=KEY_2:VALUE_2 \
      --add_tags=KEY_3:VALUE_3 \                            # Attach Policy Tags/Data Catalog tags
      --max_time_travel_hours=HOURS \                       # Set time travel window (24*[2-7] only)
      --storage_billing_model=BILLING_MODEL \               # Choose billing model (PHYSICAL | LOGICAL)
      --default_rounding_mode=ROUNDING_MODE \               # Set decimal rounding (e.g., ROUND_HALF_AWAY_FROM_ZERO)
      --external_source_access=ACCESS_TYPE \                # Enable external data source access (BigLake/Federated)
      --resource_tags=TAG_KEY:TAG_VALUE \                   # Attach Resource Manager tags for IAM/Org policies
      PROJECT_ID:DATASET_ID

..................................| 'CLIENT LIBRARY' |.....................................
from google.cloud import bigquery
client = bigquery.Client()                # Construct a BigQuery client object.
dataset_id = "project_id.your_dataset"
dataset = bigquery.Dataset(dataset_id)    # Construct a full Dataset object to send to the API. 
dataset.location = "US"                   # Location of dataset
dataset = client.create_dataset(dataset, timeout=30)  # Make an API request.
print("Created dataset {}.{}".format(client.project, dataset.dataset_id))

___________________________________________________________________________________________
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>| 'UPDATE' |<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<

.......................................| 'SQL' |...........................................
ALTER SCHEMA `project_id.my_dataset`
 SET OPTIONS (
     description = 'Description of mydataset',
     default_table_expiration_days = 3.75,
     default_partition_expiration_days = 3.75,
     default_rounding_mode = "ROUND_HALF_EVEN",
     max_time_travel_hours = 168,
     storage_billing_model = 'PHYSICAL'
);

.......................................| 'CLI' |...........................................
# Bulk Update Syntax
bq update \
      --description="NEW_DESCRIPTION" \                                  # Update metadata description
      --default_table_expiration=TABLE_EXPIRATION \                      # Update default table TTL
      --default_partition_expiration=PARTITION_EXPIRATION \              # Update default partition TTL
      --set_label=KEY_1:VALUE_1 \                                        # Add/Update label
      --max_time_travel_hours=HOURS \                                    # Update time travel window
      --storage_billing_model=BILLING_MODEL \                            # Switch storage billing type
      --default_rounding_mode=ROUNDING_MODE \                            # Update decimal rounding logic
      PROJECT_ID:DATASET_ID

# Update individual properties
bq update --description="DESCRIPTION" PROJECT_ID:DATASET_ID              # Update dataset metadata description

..................................| 'CLIENT LIBRARY' |.....................................
from google.cloud import bigquery
client = bigquery.Client()
dataset_id = 'your-project.your_dataset'
dataset = client.get_dataset(dataset_id)     # 1. Fetch the current state
dataset.description = "Updated description." # 2. Update properties
dataset.default_table_expiration_ms = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000  # 1 day
dataset.default_partition_expiration_ms = 48 * 60 * 60 * 1000
dataset.labels = {"dept": "finance", "status": "prod"}
dataset.max_time_travel_hours = 48  # Must be 48, 72, 96, 120, 144, 168
dataset.storage_billing_model = "PHYSICAL" # Or "LOGICAL"
dataset.default_rounding_mode = "ROUND_HALF_AWAY_FROM_ZERO"

dataset = client.update_dataset(dataset, [
    "description", 
    "default_table_expiration_ms",
    "default_partition_expiration_ms",
    "labels",
    "max_time_travel_hours",
    "storage_billing_model",
    "default_rounding_mode"
]) 
print(f"Successfully updated {dataset_id}")

___________________________________________________________________________________________
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>| 'DELETE' |<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<

.......................................| 'SQL' |...........................................
DROP SCHEMA `project_id.my_dataset`;                   # By default, this only works to delete an empty dataset.
DROP SCHEMA `project_id.my_dataset` CASCADE;           # To delete a dataset and all of its contents, use the CASCADE keyword
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS `project_id.my_dataset` CASCADE; # Safe delete

.......................................| 'CLI' |...........................................
bq rm -d project_id.my_dataset        # deletes empty dataset 
bq rm -r -d project_id.my_dataset     # deletes non-empty dataset 
bq rm -r -f -d project_id.my_dataset  # delete dataset without prompt

..................................| 'CLIENT LIBRARY' |.....................................
from google.cloud import bigquery
client = bigquery.Client()
dataset_id = 'your-project.your_dataset'
client.delete_dataset(
    dataset_id, 
    delete_contents=True,  # delete_contents=True: Deletes all tables/views inside (equivalent to CASCADE).
    not_found_ok=True      # not_found_ok=True: Does not raise an error if the dataset is already deleted.   
)
print(f"Deleted dataset {dataset_id}")

__________________________________________________________________________________________
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>| ' TIMETRAVEL RESTORE' |<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<

.......................................| 'SQL' |...........................................
CREATE TABLE my_dataset.restored_table
AS SELECT * FROM `my_project.my_dataset.deleted_table`
FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 1 HOUR);

.......................................| 'CLI' |...........................................
bq cp --snapshot_time 1625000000000 source_project:dataset.table restored_table

..................................| 'CLIENT LIBRARY' |.....................................

__________________________________________________________________________________________
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>| 'LIST DATASET' |<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<

.......................................| 'SQL' |...........................................
SELECT schema_name FROM PROJECT_ID.`region-REGION`.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SCHEMATA; 

.......................................| 'CLI' |...........................................
bq ls            # All datasets in the default project
bq ls project_id # All datasets under mentioned project
bq ls -a         # All datasets including hidden
bq ls -n 100     # All datasets upto mentioned number
bq ls --filter labels.department:marketing # with specified labels only

..................................| 'CLIENT LIBRARY' |.....................................
from google.cloud import bigquery
client = bigquery.Client()
datasets = list(client.list_datasets()) # list_datasets() returns an iterator of DatasetListItem objects
if datasets:
    print(f"Datasets in project {client.project}:")
    for ds in datasets:
        print(f"\t- {ds.dataset_id}")   # ds.dataset_id only provides the ID, not the full project path
else:
    print(f"Project {client.project} contains no datasets.")

__________________________________________________________________________________________
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>| 'COPY DATASET' |<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<

.......................................| 'SQL' |...........................................
ALTER SCHEMA `my_project.my_dataset`
ADD REPLICA `my_replica_name`
OPTIONS(location = 'us-east4');

.......................................| 'CLI' |...........................................
bq mk --transfer_config \
    --project_id=dest-project-id \
    --data_source=cross_region_copy \ #Note: The data_source is always cross_region_copy even if you are copying within the same region.
    --target_dataset="dest_dataset" \
    --display_name="My Dataset Copy" \
    --params='{"source_dataset_id":"'source_dataset'","source_project_id":"'source-project-id'","overwrite_destination_table":"true"}'

..................................| 'CLIENT LIBRARY' |.....................................
from google.cloud import bigquery_datatransfer
client = bigquery_datatransfer.DataTransferServiceClient()
project_id = "my-destination-project"
dataset_id = "my_destination_dataset"
transfer_config = bigquery_datatransfer.TransferConfig(
    destination_dataset_id=dataset_id,
    display_name="One-time Dataset Copy",
    data_source_id="cross_region_copy",
    params={
        "source_project_id": "my-source-project",
        "source_dataset_id": "my_source_dataset",
        "overwrite_destination_table": True,
    },
    schedule="every 24 hours", # You can disable this after the first run
)
transfer_config = client.create_transfer_config(
    parent=client.common_project_path(project_id),
    transfer_config=transfer_config,
)
print(f"Created transfer config: {transfer_config.name}")

Routines.description:
Routines

BigQuery supports the following routines:

  • User-defined functions (UDFs)
  • User-defined aggregate functions (UDAFs)
  • Table functions
  • Remote functions
  • Stored procedures

1. User-defined functions (UDFs)

A User-Defined Function (UDF) allows you to extend BigQueryâ€™s built-in functionality. You can write them using SQL, JavaScript, or Python (via Remote Functions). UDFs take -zero or more input columns and return a single value (scalar) or a set of values (table-valued).

Temporary UDFs

-- Scope: Limited to the current session or multi-statement query. They disappear once the script finishes.

-- Best Use Case: Ad-hoc data cleaning or complex logic specific to a single report that doesn't need to be shared with the team.

-- Syntax Note: Use CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION. You do not need to specify a dataset.

-- Management: DROP FUNCTION is only required if you want to remove it mid-script; otherwise, it cleans itself up.

Persistent UDFs

-- Scope: Stored in a specific BigQuery Dataset. They can be called by anyone with the right permissions, indefinitely.

-- Best Use Case: Business logic used across multiple projects, such as a custom currency converter or a standard email-masking tool.

-- Syntax Note: Use CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION project_id.dataset.function_name.

-- Management: Use DROP FUNCTION project_id.dataset.function_name to delete it manually.

Templated (Polymorphic) UDFs

BigQuery allows for "type-agnostic" functions using the ANY TYPE argument.

-- Flexibility: A single function can handle INT64, FLOAT64, or STRING inputs without rewriting the logic.

-- Strict Return Types: While inputs can be flexible, the return type must be a concrete data type or inferred automatically from the SQL expression. It cannot be ANY TYPE.

-- Validation: Errors occur at call time if the logic inside the function (e.g., a mathematical multiplication) is applied to an incompatible type (e.g., a String).


1. SQL The "Performance First" Choice

SQL UDFs are native to the BigQuery engine. They are essentially macros that the optimizer can "inline" into the main execution plan.

CAPABILITIES

Supports Templated Parameters (ANY TYPE) for polymorphic logic.

Can be Scalar (returns one value) or Table-Valued (returns a full result set).

Highest execution speed and best integration with the query optimizer.

LIMITATIONS

Limited to logic expressible in Standard SQL (no complex loops or external library imports).

Recursive calls are not supported.

WHERE TO USE

- 90% of use cases. Use for reusable business logic, math formulas, and complex string manipulations.

WHY

- They are free of additional overhead. They use the same slots as your query and are the most cost-effective.


2. JavaScript The "Complex Logic" Choice

When SQL expressions become unreadable or impossible (e.g., deep nested JSON parsing or custom encryption), JavaScript is the middle ground.

CAPABILITIES

External Libraries: Can import heavy JS libraries (like CryptoJS or Moment.js) via Google Cloud Storage.

Regex & JSON: Handles sophisticated regular expressions and deep object manipulation more gracefully than SQL.

LIMITATIONS

Performance Hit: Runs in a restricted "V8" engine environment, which adds latency and consumes more slot resources.

Memory Constraints: High-memory JS tasks can cause "Out of Memory" errors that crash the query.

No Network Access: Cannot call external APIs or fetch data outside the query.

WHERE

Complex data transformations, legacy JS logic migration, or when using existing JS math/string libraries.

WHY

Provides a bridge for logic that is too "procedural" for SQL to handle efficiently.


3. Python The "Data Science & Integration" Choice

The newest addition to the UDF family, Python UDFs run on managed infrastructure and offer the most power.

CAPABILITIES

Vectorization: Processes batches of rows (via pandas.Series or DataFrame) instead of one-by-one, significantly boosting performance for large datasets.

PyPI Ecosystem: Directly install third-party packages (like scipy, numpy, or pandas) via the packages option.

Remote Connections: Can be used as "Remote Functions" to access external GCP services (Vertex AI, Cloud Functions, etc.).

LIMITATIONS

Persistent Only: No support for TEMP functions; they must be saved to a dataset.

Caching: Query results are never cached because Python logic is treated as non-deterministic.

Type Constraints: Does not support JSON, GEOGRAPHY, or INTERVAL types.

Cold Starts: Initial execution may be slower due to container spin-up time.

WHERE

Advanced statistical modeling, machine learning inference within a query, or when you need a specific Python-only library.

WHY

It eliminates the need to move data out of BigQuery into a notebook for advanced processing.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
********************************| 'CREATION' |********************************

...............................| 'SQL UDF' |.............................
# â€”â€”â€” Temporary â€”â€”â€”
CREATE TEMP FUNCTION AddFourAndDivide(x INT64, y INT64)
RETURNS FLOAT64 AS ((x + 4) / y);

# â€”â€”â€” Persistent â€”â€”â€”
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION mydataset.AddFourAndDivide(x INT64, y INT64)
RETURNS FLOAT64 AS ((x + 4) / y);

# â€”â€”â€” Templated (Polymorphic) â€”â€”â€”
CREATE TEMP FUNCTION AddFourAndDivideAny(x ANY TYPE, y ANY TYPE)
AS ((x + 4) / y);

# â€”â€”â€” Table-Valued (TVF) â€”â€”â€”
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE FUNCTION mydataset.NamesAfterYear(yr INT64)
AS (
  SELECT name, state
  FROM `bigquery-public-data.usa_names.usa_1910_current`
  WHERE year > yr
);


.............................| 'JAVASCRIPT UDF' |............................
# â€”â€”â€” Temporary â€”â€”â€”
CREATE TEMP FUNCTION MultiplyInputs(x FLOAT64, y FLOAT64)
RETURNS FLOAT64 LANGUAGE js AS r"""
  return x * y;
""";

# â€”â€”â€” Persistent â€”â€”â€”
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION mydataset.MultiplyInputs(x FLOAT64, y FLOAT64)
RETURNS FLOAT64 LANGUAGE js AS r"""
  return x * y;
""";

# â€”â€”â€” With External Libraries â€”â€”â€”
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION mydataset.MyFunc(a FLOAT64, b STRING)
RETURNS STRING LANGUAGE js
OPTIONS (library=['gs://my-bucket/path/to/lib1.js',
                  'gs://my-bucket/path/to/lib2.js'])
AS r"""
  return doInterestingStuff(a, b);
""";

...............................| 'PYTHON UDF' |..............................
# â€”â€”â€” Basic Persistent (Python only supports persistent) â€”â€”â€”
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION `PROJECT_ID.DATASET_ID`.MultiplyInputs(
  x FLOAT64, y FLOAT64)
RETURNS FLOAT64 LANGUAGE python
OPTIONS(runtime_version='python-3.11', entry_point='multiply')
AS r'''
  def multiply(x, y):
    return x * y
''';

# â€”â€”â€” Vectorized (Batch Processing) â€”â€”â€”
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION `PROJECT_ID.DATASET_ID`.MultiplyVectorized(
  x FLOAT64, y FLOAT64)
RETURNS FLOAT64 LANGUAGE python
OPTIONS(runtime_version='python-3.11', entry_point='vectorized_multiply')
AS r'''
  import pandas as pd
  def vectorized_multiply(df: pd.DataFrame):
    return df['x'] * df['y']
''';

# â€”â€”â€” With Third-Party Packages (PyPI) â€”â€”â€”
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION `PROJECT_ID.DATASET_ID`.CircleArea(radius FLOAT64)
RETURNS FLOAT64 LANGUAGE python
OPTIONS(entry_point='area_handler', runtime_version='python-3.11',
        packages=['scipy==1.15.3'])
AS r"""
  import scipy
  def area_handler(radius):
    return scipy.constants.pi * radius * radius
""";

# â€”â€”â€” With External Python Library Files â€”â€”â€”
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION `PROJECT_ID.DATASET_ID`.MyFunc(a FLOAT64, b STRING)
RETURNS STRING LANGUAGE python

2. AGREGATE UDFs

A UDAF lets you create an aggregate function by using an expression that contains code. A UDAF accepts columns of input, performs a calculation on a group of rows at a time, and then returns the result of that calculation as a single value.

You can create a SQL UDAF that is persistent, meaning that you can reuse the UDAF across multiple queries. Persistent UDAFs are safe to call when they are shared between owners.

UDAFs can't mutate data, talk to external systems, or send logs to Google Cloud Observability or similar applications.

To create a persistent UDAF, use the CREATE AGGREGATE FUNCTION statement without the TEMP or TEMPORARY keyword. You must include the dataset in the function path.

Use aggregate and non-aggregate parameters

You can create a SQL UDAF that has both aggregate and non-aggregate parameters.

UDAFs normally aggregate function parameters across all rows in a group. However, you can specify a function parameter as non-aggregate with the NOT AGGREGATE keyword.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
********************************| 'CREATION' |********************************

...............................| 'SQL TEMP' |.............................
CREATE TEMP AGGREGATE FUNCTION ScaledAverage(val FLOAT64, divisor FLOAT64)
RETURNS FLOAT64
AS (AVG(val / divisor));
...............................| 'SQL PERSISTENT' |.............................
CREATE OR REPLACE AGGREGATE FUNCTION mydataset.WeightedAverage(val FLOAT64, weight INT64) 
RETURNS FLOAT64 
AS (SUM(val * weight) / SUM(weight));

...............................| 'WITH NOT AGGREGATE PARAMETER' |.............................
CREATE OR REPLACE AGGREGATE FUNCTION mydataset.ScaledSum(
  val FLOAT64, 
  multiplier FLOAT64 NOT AGGREGATE)
RETURNS FLOAT64
AS (SUM(val) * multiplier);

...............................| 'JAVASCRIPT TEMP' |.............................
CREATE OR REPLACE AGGREGATE FUNCTION mydataset.LongestString(str STRING)
RETURNS STRING
LANGUAGE js
AS r"""
  export function initialState() { return {max_str: ""}; }
  export function aggregate(state, str) {
    if (str && str.length > state.max_str.length) 
      { state.max_str = str;}
  }
  export function merge(state, partialState) {
    if (partialState.max_str.length > state.max_str.length) {
      state.max_str = partialState.max_str;}
  }
  export function finalize(state) { return state.max_str;}
""";
...............................| 'JAVASCRIPT PERSISTENT' |.............................

RETURNS STRING
LANGUAGE js
AS r"""

#Create a persistent JavaScript UDAF


3. TABLE FUNCTIONS

A table function, also called a table-valued function (TVF), is a user-defined function that returns a table. You can use a table function anywhere that you can use a table. Table functions behave similarly to views, but a table function can take parameters.

To create a table function, use the CREATE TABLE FUNCTION statement. A table function contains a query that produces a table. The function returns the query result. 

We can JOIN, SUBQUERY TVFs

LIMITATIONS

  • The query body must be a SELECT statement and cannot modify anything. DDL, and DML statements are not allowed in table functions.
  • Table functions must be stored in the same location as the tables they reference.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE FUNCTION mydataset.names_by_year(y INT64)
AS (
  SELECT year, name, SUM(number) AS total
  FROM `bigquery-public-data.usa_names.usa_1910_current`
  WHERE year = y
  GROUP BY year, name
);
#USAGE
SELECT * FROM mydataset.names_by_year(1950) ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 5


#Table as input to TVF
CREATE TABLE FUNCTION mydataset.compute_sales ( orders TABLE<sales INT64, item STRING>, item_name STRING)
AS (
  SELECT SUM(sales) AS total_sales, item
  FROM orders
  WHERE item = item_name
  GROUP BY item
);

#DELETE
DROP TABLE FUNCTION mydataset.names_by_year


3. REMOTE FUNCTIONS

A BigQuery remote function allows you to implement your function in other languages than SQL and Javascript or with the libraries or services which are not allowed in BigQuery user-defined functions.

A BigQuery remote function lets you incorporate GoogleSQL functionality with software outside of BigQuery by providing a direct integration with Cloud Run functions and Cloud Run. With BigQuery remote functions, you can deploy your functions in Cloud Run functions or Cloud Run implemented with any supported language, and then invoke them from GoogleSQL queries.

Workflow

  1. Create the HTTP endpoint in Cloud Run functions or Cloud Run.
  2. Create a remote function in BigQuery.
  3. Create a connection of type CLOUD_RESOURCE.
  4. Create a remote function.
  5. Use the remote function in a query just like any other user-defined functions.

LIMITATIONS

  • Remote functions do not support ARRAY, STRUCT, INTERVAL, or GEOGRAPHY types.
  • You cannot create table-valued remote functions.
  • You cannot use remote functions when creating materialized views.
  • The return value of a remote function is always assumed to be non-deterministic so the result of a query calling a remote function is not cached.

4. STORED PROCEDURE

A stored procedure is a collection of statements that can be called from other queries or other stored procedures. A procedure can take input arguments and return values as output. You name and store a procedure in a BigQuery dataset. A stored procedure can access or modify data across multiple datasets by multiple users. It can also contain a multi-statement query.

Some stored procedures are built into BigQuery and don't need to be created. These are called system procedures 

Stored procedures support procedural language statements, which let you do things like define variables and implement control flow.

CREATE

To create a procedure, use the CREATE PROCEDURE statement. the body of the procedure appears between BEGIN and END statements

If neither IN, OUT, nor INOUT is specified, the argument is treated as an IN argument.

#SYNTAX
CREATE PROCEDURE dataset_name.procedure_name()
BEGIN
-- statements here
END

#EXAMPLE
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE mydataset.create_customer()
BEGIN
  DECLARE id STRING;
  SET id = GENERATE_UUID();
  INSERT INTO mydataset.customers (customer_id)
    VALUES(id);
  SELECT FORMAT("Created customer %s", id);
END

#CALL
CALL mydataset.create_customer();


Pass a value in with an input parameter

A procedure can have input parameters. An input parameter allows input for a procedure, but does not allow output.

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE mydataset.create_customer(name STRING)
BEGIN
  DECLARE id STRING;
  SET id = GENERATE_UUID();
  INSERT INTO mydataset.customers (customer_id, name)
    VALUES(id, name);
  SELECT FORMAT("Created customer %s (%s)", id, name);
END


Pass a value out with an output parameter

A procedure can have output parameters. An output parameter returns a value from the procedure, but does not allow input for the procedure. To create an output parameter, use the OUT keyword before the name of the parameter.

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE mydataset.create_customer(name STRING, OUT id STRING)
BEGIN
  SET id = GENERATE_UUID();
  INSERT INTO mydataset.customers (customer_id, name)
    VALUES(id, name);
  SELECT FORMAT("Created customer %s (%s)", id, name);
END

#To call this procedure, you must use a variable to receive the output value:

--- Create a new customer record.
DECLARE id STRING;
CALL mydataset.create_customer("alice",id);

--- Display the record.
SELECT * FROM mydataset.customers
WHERE customer_id = id;


Pass a value in and out with an input/output parameter

A procedure can also have input/output parameters. An input/output parameter returns a value from the procedure and also accepts input for the procedure. To create an input/output parameter, use the INOUT keyword before the name of the parameter

CREATE PROCEDURE mydataset.AddDelta(INOUT x INT64, delta INT64)
BEGIN
  SET x = x + delta;
END;

#CALL
DECLARE accumulator INT64 DEFAULT 0;
CALL mydataset.AddDelta(accumulator, 5);
CALL mydataset.AddDelta(accumulator, 3);
SELECT accumulator;

#OUTPUT
+-------------+
| accumulator |
+-------------+
|           8 |
+-------------+

Search Indexes.description:
Search & Vector Index


Search Indexes

BigQuery search indexes let you use GoogleSQL to efficiently find unique data elements that are buried in unstructured text and semi-structured JSON data, without having to know the table schemas in advance.

BigQuery stores and manages your indexes, so that when data becomes available in BigQuery, you can immediately retrieve it with the SEARCH function or other operators and functions, such as the equal (=), IN, or LIKE operators and certain string and JSON functions. 

USE CASES:

-- Search system, network, or application logs stored in BigQuery tables.

-- Identify data elements for deletion to comply with regulatory processes.

-- Support developer troubleshooting.

-- Perform security audits.

-- Create a dashboard that requires highly selective search filters.

-- Search pre-processed data for exact matches.

LIMITATIONS

-- Cannot create a search index directly on a view or materialized view (but SEARCH on a view of an indexed table does use the underlying index)

-- Cannot create a search index on an external table

-- Renaming a table after creating a search index invalidates the index

-- Fuzzy searching, typo correction, wildcards, and document-style search are not available

-- If the search index is not yet at 100% coverage, you are still charged for all index storage reported in INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SEARCH_INDEXES

-- Search indexes are not used when the query references Materialized Views

-- Search indexes are not used in multi-statement transaction queries

-- Search indexes are not used in time-travel queries

REFRESH

Search indexes are fully managed by BigQuery and automatically refreshed when the table changes. A full refresh can happen when:

-- Partition expiration is updated

-- An indexed column is updated due to a schema change

-- The index is stale due to a lack of BACKGROUND reservation slots for incremental refreshes

SEARCH FUNCTION BEHAVIOR

-- Case-insensitive: SEARCH(table, 'Apple') matches "apple", "APPLE", etc.

-- Tokenized: the search term is split into tokens using the index's analyzer; all tokens must match

-- Exact token match only: no fuzzy search, wildcards, typo correction, or stemming

-- Point lookup optimized: designed for selective, needle-in-a-haystack queries â€” not full-document scans

BQ BEHAVIOR ON INDEX

-- If an indexed column's data is updated in every row (e.g., during a backfill), the whole index needs to be updated â€” equivalent to a full refresh. Perform backfills slowly (partition by partition) to minimize impact.

-- If any schema change prevents an explicitly indexed column from being indexed, the index is permanently disabled.

-- If you delete the only indexed column or rename the table, the search index is deleted automatically.

-- If you create a search index on a table smaller than 10 GB, the index is not populated.

-- If indexed table data falls below 10 GB, the index is temporarily disabled (IndexUnusedReason: BASE_TABLE_TOO_SMALL).

ANALYZER TYPES

-- LOG_ANALYZER â€” best for logs, splits on non-alphanumeric characters (default)

-- TEXT_ANALYZER â€” best for natural language / prose

-- NO_OP_ANALYZER â€” treats the entire string as one token (exact match only)

-- PATTERN_ANALYZER â€” custom regex-based splitting

INFORMATION SCHEMA

-- The INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SEARCH_INDEXES view has information on each search index created on a dataset.

-- The INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SEARCH_INDEX_COLUMNS view has information on which columns of each table in the dataset are indexed.

-- The INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SEARCH_INDEXES_BY_ORGANIZATION view has information on search indexes for the whole organization associated with the current project.


Vector Indexes

While a Search Index is for finding exact words or IDs (like Ctrl+F), a Vector Index is for finding meaning and similarity.

It is the engine behind "AI-style" search. Instead of looking for the exact letters "Apple," a vector index can find "iPhone," "fruit," or "MacBook" because it understands they are conceptually related.

EMBEDDINGS

-- To use a vector index, first convert your data (text, images, or audio) into embeddings

-- An embedding is a long list of numbers (a vector), e.g., [0.12, -0.05, 0.88, ...]

-- These numbers represent "coordinates" in a multi-dimensional space â€” similar things are placed close together

WHEN TO USE

-- Recommendation Systems: "Users who bought this also likedâ€¦"

-- Semantic Search: Building a search bar that understands intent, not just spelling

-- Image/Audio Retrieval: Finding similar files based on visual/audio features

-- AI Context (RAG): Providing your AI model the most relevant documents from your database to answer a question

DISTANCE TYPES

-- COSINEMeasures angle between vectors; best for text/semantic similarity

-- EUCLIDEANMeasures straight-line distance; good for numeric feature spaces

-- DOT_PRODUCTInner product; fastest when vectors are normalized

INDEX TYPES

-- IVFInverted File Index â€” clusters vectors into lists for fast approximate search; supports num_lists option

-- TREE_AHTree + Asymmetric Hashing â€” alternative ANN method


____________________________________________________________________________________________________
*****************************************| 'CREATION' |*********************************************

.......................| 'SEARCH INDEX - BASIC' |........................................
#Base Table: simple_table(a STRING, b INT64, c JSON);
CREATE SEARCH INDEX my_index
[
ON dataset.simple_table(a, c); 
#OR
ON dataset.simple_table(ALL COLUMNS);
] 
.............................| 'SEARCH INDEX WITH LOG_ANALYZER' |...................................
CREATE SEARCH INDEX my_index
ON dataset.simple_table(a)
OPTIONS (analyzer = 'LOG_ANALYZER'); 

...........................| 'SEARCH INDEX WITH PATTERN_ANALYZER' |.................................
CREATE SEARCH INDEX my_index
ON dataset.simple_table(a)
OPTIONS (
  analyzer = 'PATTERN_ANALYZER',
  analyzer_options = '{"patterns": ["[a-zA-Z0-9]+"]}' -- custom token-splitting regex
);

..........................| 'SEARCH INDEX WITH DATATYPE-FILTER' |...................................
#Base Table: simple_table(a STRING, b INT64, c JSON, d TIMESTAMP);
#INDEX WITH DATATYPE MENTIONED
CREATE SEARCH INDEX my_index
ON dataset.simple_table(a, b, c, d)
OPTIONS ( data_types = ['STRING', 'INT64', 'TIMESTAMP']);

Tables.description:
Tables

A BigQuery table contains individual records organized in rows. Each record is composed of columns (also called fields).

Every table is defined by a schema that describes the column names, data types, and other information.

You can specify the schema of a table when it is created, or you can create a table without a schema and declare the schema in the query job or load job that first populates it with data.

1. Standard BigQuery Tables

These are the "native" tables where data is fully managed by Google.

-- Storage: Googleâ€™s proprietary Capacitor columnar format.

-- Key Advantage: Offers the best query performance and supports full DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and ACID transactions.

-- Optimization: Supports Partitioning and Clustering to reduce costs and speed up scans.

-- Best For: Frequently queried production data and high-performance analytics.

2. External Tables

Data remains in its original location; BigQuery only stores the metadata (schema).

A. BigLake Tables

-- Storage: Cloud Storage, AWS S3, or Azure Blob Storage (usually in Parquet, Avro, or ORC).

-- Key Advantage: Uses Service Accounts to access data, meaning users don't need direct permissions to the underlying filesâ€”only to the BigLake table.

-- Missing Info: Supports Metadata Caching, which significantly boosts performance compared to standard external tables.

-- Best For: Hybrid/Multi-cloud "Data Lakehouses" and strictly governed datasets.

B. Object Tables

-- Storage: Cloud Storage (Unstructured data like images, PDFs, audio, or CSVs).

-- Key Advantage: Provides a structured SQL interface to unstructured data. It treats each file as a row with metadata (size, created time, URI).

-- Integration: Can be used with Vertex AI for machine learning (e.g., performing inference on images via SQL).

-- Best For: Managing AI/ML training data and analyzing file metadata.

C. Non-BigLake External Tables

-- Storage: Cloud Storage, Google Drive, Bigtable, or AlloyDB.

-- Key Advantage: Quickest way to query data without an ETL process.

-- The Catch: Performance is generally slower because BigQuery has to fetch data over the network for every query. It also lacks row-level security.

-- Best For: Small, frequently changing files (like a Google Sheet for manual lookups) or one-time data explorations.


CRUD OPERATIONS

BQ CLI


bq mk \
--table \
--description "Human-readable description of the table" \
--expiration 0 \
--label key:value \
--label key2:value2 \
location
--location us-east1 \
time-partitioning
--time_partitioning_filed transaction_date \
--time_partitioning_filed DAY \
--time_partitioning_expiration 604800 \
--require_partition_filter=true \
integer-range-partitioning
--range_partitioning=customer_id,0,1000,100 \
clustering
--clustering_fields col1,col2,col3,col4 \
encryption
--destination_kms_key projects/my-project/locations/us/keyRings/my-ring/cryptoKeys/my-key \
schema
--schema 'col1:TYPE:MODE,col2:TYPE:MODE,...' \
json-schema-file
/tmp/schema.json \
project:dataset.table

    field="date",  # name of column to use for partitioning
    expiration_ms=1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 90,
)  # 90 days

table = client.create_table(table)
print(
    f"Created table {table.project}.{table.dataset_id}.{table.table_id}, "
    f"partitioned on column {table.time_partitioning.field}."
)

from google.cloud import bigquery

client = bigquery.Client() # Construct a BigQuery client object.

    bigquery.SchemaField("full_name", "STRING"),
    bigquery.SchemaField("city", "STRING"),
    bigquery.SchemaField("zipcode", "INTEGER"),
]

table = bigquery.Table(table_id, schema=schema)
table.range_partitioning = bigquery.RangePartitioning(
    field="zipcode",  # NULLABLE column with INTEGER / INT64 data type.
    range_=bigquery.PartitionRange(start=0, end=100000, interval=10),
)
table = client.create_table(table)  # Make an API request.
print("Created table {}.{}.{}".format(table.project, table.dataset_id, table.table_id))

4. By defining a table that references an external data source.


5. While loading data

When you load data into BigQuery, you can load data into a new table or partition, you can append data to an existing table or partition, or you can overwrite a table or partition. You don't need to create an empty table before loading data into it. You can create the new table and load your data at the same time.

6. DDL statement.

CREATE TABLE mydataset.newtable
(
  x INT64 OPTIONS(description="An optional INTEGER field"),
  y STRUCT <
    a ARRAY <STRING> OPTIONS(description="A repeated STRING field"),
    b BOOLv>
)
PARTITION BY _PARTITIONDATE
OPTIONS(
  expiration_timestamp=TIMESTAMP "2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC",
  partition_expiration_days=1,
  description="a table that expires in 2025, with each partition living for 24 hours",
  labels=[("org_unit", "development")]
)

Modifying table schemas:

1. Add a column:

You can add columns to an existing table's schema definition by using one of the following options:

1. Add a new empty column.

Issue the bq update command and provide a JSON schema file, the columns must be NULLABLE or REPEATED.

You cannot add a REQUIRED column to an existing table schema. Adding a REQUIRED column to an existing table schema in the API or bq command-line tool causes an error.

REQUIRED columns can be added only when you create a table while loading data, or when you create an empty table with a schema definition.

You can also update record data by adding the new column mode, name and type to the firlds section of the record type column in the dchema file.

#syntax
bq update PROJECT_ID:DATASET.TABLE SCHEMA
#example
bq update mydataset.mytable /tmp/myschema.json

2. Overwrite a table with a load or query job.

You can add new columns to an existing table when you load data into it and choose to overwrite the existing table.

When you overwrite an existing table, the schema of the data you're loading is used to overwrite the existing table's schema.

2.1 Add columns in a load append job:

The new schema is determined by one of the following:

  • Autodetection (for CSV and JSON files)
  • A schema specified in a JSON schema file (for CSV and JSON files)
  • The self-describing source data for Avro, ORC, Parquet and Datastore export files

Use the bq load command to load your data and specify the --noreplace

If the data you're appending is in CSV or newline-delimited JSON format, specify the --autodetect flag to use schema auto-detection or supply the schema in a JSON schema file.

Set the --schema_update_option flag to ALLOW_FIELD_ADDITION to indicate that the data you're appending contains new columns.

bq load \
--noreplace \
--schema_update_option=ALLOW_FIELD_ADDITION \
--source_format=AVRO \
mydataset.mytable \
/tmp/mydata.avro

2.2 Add columns in a query append job

When you add columns using an append operation in a query job, the schema of the query results is used to update the schema of the destination table. Note that you cannot query a table in one location and write the results to a table in another location.

Use the bq query command to query your data and specify the --destination_table flag to indicate which table you're appending.

Set the --schema_update_option flag to ALLOW_FIELD_ADDITION to indicate that the query results you're appending contain new columns.

bq query \
--destination_table mydataset.mytable2 \
--append_table \
--schema_update_option=ALLOW_FIELD_ADDITION \
--use_legacy_sql=false \
'SELECT column1,column2 FROM mydataset.mytable'

2. Change a column's name

To rename a column on a table, use the ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN DDL statement. The following example renames the column old_name to new_name on mytable

ALTER TABLE mydataset.mytable RENAME COLUMN old_name TO new_name;

3. Change a column's data type

Changing a column's data type isn't supported by the Google Cloud console, the bq command-line tool, or the BigQuery API. If you attempt to update a table by applying a schema that specifies a new data type for a column, an error is returned.

3.1 Change a column's data type with a DDL statement

The following example creates a table with a column of type INT64, then updates the type to NUMERIC:

CREATE TABLE mydataset.mytable(c1 INT64);

ALTER TABLE mydataset.mytable
ALTER COLUMN c1 SET DATA TYPE NUMERIC;

2. Table clones

which are lightweight, writeable copies of BigQuery tables. BigQuery only stores the delta between a table clone and its base table.

3. Table snapshots

which are point-in-time copies of tables. They are read-only, but you can restore a table from a table snapshot. 




NAMING:

  • Contain characters with a total of up to 1,024 UTF-8 bytes.
  • Contain Unicode characters in category L (letter), M (mark), N (number), Pc (connector, including underscore), Pd (dash), Zs (space). For more information
  • Table names are case-sensitive by default. mytable and MyTable can coexist in the same dataset, unless they are part of a dataset with case-sensitivity turned off.
  • Some table names and table name prefixes are reserved. If you receive an error saying that your table name or prefix is reserved, then select a different name and try again.
  • If you include multiple dot operators (.) in a sequence, the duplicate operators are implicitly stripped.
  • For example, this: project_name....dataset_name..table_name Becomes this: project_name.dataset_name.table_name

CONTROL ACCESS:

https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/column-level-security-intro

You can also restrict data access within tables, by using the following methods:

1. column-level access control

BigQuery provides fine-grained access to sensitive columns using policy tags, or type-based classification, of data. Using BigQuery column-level access control, you can create policies that check, at query time, whether a user has proper access. 

To restrict data access at the column level:

  • Define a taxonomy and policy tags. Create and manage a taxonomy and policy tags for your data. 
  • Assign policy tags to your BigQuery columns. In BigQuery, use schema annotations to assign a policy tag to each column where you want to restrict access.
  • Enforce access control on the taxonomy. Enforcing access control causes the access restrictions defined for all of the policy tags in the taxonomy to be applied.
  • Manage access on the policy tags. Use Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies to restrict access to each policy tag. The policy is in effect for each column that belongs to the policy tag.

When a user tries to access column data at query time, BigQuery checks the column policy tag and its policy to see whether the user is authorized to access the data.


  • column data masking
  • row-level security

Required permissions

At a minimum, to get information about tables, you must be granted bigquery.tables.get permissions. The following predefined IAM roles include bigquery.tables.get permissions:

  • bigquery.metadataViewer
  • bigquery.dataViewer
  • bigquery.dataOwner
  • bigquery.dataEditor
  • bigquery.admin

In addition, if a user has bigquery.datasets.create permissions, when that user creates a dataset, they are granted bigquery.dataOwner access to it. bigquery.dataOwner access gives the user the ability to retrieve table metadata.


Table limitations

BigQuery tables are subject to the following limitations:

  • Table names must be unique per dataset.
  • When you export BigQuery table data, the only supported destination is Cloud Storage.
  • When you use an API call, enumeration performance slows as you approach 50,000 tables in a dataset.
  • The Google Cloud console can display up to 50,000 tables for each dataset.

Views.description:
VIEWS

In modern data warehousing, views serve as an important abstraction layer between raw data and business intelligence.

Within BigQuery, architects typically choose between two types:

  1. Logical (standard) views and
  2. Materialized views.

While these views share a common interface, their underlying mechanics, performance profiles, and cost implications differ.


1. Logical views

A logical (standard) view is a virtual table defined by a SQL query. It does not store any physical data; instead, it stores the query logic required to retrieve data from the underlying base tables.

When you query a logical view, the BigQuery query engine expands the view into its underlying query. This process means BigQuery re-executes the view every time it is called.

BigQuery merges your view definition and query filter into a single optimized query, evaluates the combined WHERE clause at planning time, and scans zero bytes if conditions are contradictory.


LIMITATIONS

Views are read-only. For example, you can't run queries that insert, update, or delete data.

The dataset that contains your view and the dataset that contains the tables referenced by the view must be in the same location.

You cannot reference query parameters in views. -- we can use Stored procedure if parameters are needed.

BigQuery supports up to 16 levels of nested views. Creating views up to this limit is possible, but querying is limited to 15 levels. If the limit is exceeded, BigQuery returns an INVALID_INPUT error.

A single GoogleSQL query that defines a view can be up to 256 K characters long. This limit applies to a single query and does not include the length of the views referenced in the query.

When you add a description to a view, the text can be at most 16,384 characters.


BENIFITS

No storage overhead: Because no additional data is stored, you pay only for the storage of the base tables.

Real-time accuracy: Because the query runs at execution time, results always reflect the most current state of the base tables.

Logical abstraction: Simplifies complex joins or applies row-level security without duplicating data.

SQL flexibility: Supports the full range of BigQuery SQL, including complex window functions, user-defined functions (UDFs), and all join types.


USAGE

Semantic layering Rename complex column names into business-friendly terms for non-technical users.

Rapid development Use when logic is in flux and you don't want to manage the overhead of physical storage.

Consolidated data sources Provide a data source for visualization tools such as Looker Studio or BigQuery sharing (formerly Analytics Hub).


2. Materialized views

Materialized views are precomputed views that periodically store the results of a SQL query. Unlike logical views, they physically store the computed data, which lets BigQuery serve results faster without repeatedly processing the raw base data. This can reduce query latency for large datasets by pre-processing queries and can reduce compute costs for frequently used queries.


REFRESH BEHAVIOR

Automatic refresh: When enable_refresh=true, BigQuery automatically refreshes the MV at the specified interval (default: 30 minutes).

Manual refresh: Use CALL BQ.REFRESH_MATERIALIZED_VIEW() to force an immediate refresh.

Smart refresh: BigQuery performs incremental refreshes when possible (appends/updates to base tables), but falls back to full refresh for complex changes.

Staleness tolerance: Use max_staleness option to allow queries to use slightly outdated MV data if the MV hasn't refreshed recently, rather than falling back to base tables.


QUERY REWRITING

BigQuery automatically determines whether to use the materialized view or base tables:

- Uses MV: When the query can be answered entirely by the MV data

- Uses base tables: When MV is too stale, incomplete, or doesn't cover the query pattern

- Hybrid: May combine MV data with base table scans for optimal performance

You can verify which approach was used in the Query Execution Details.


PARTITIONING BEHAVIOR

- MVs can define their OWN partitioning scheme (doesn't have to match base table)

- Example: Base table partitioned by timestamp, MV partitioned by DATE(timestamp)

- However, for BigLake tables, MV partitioning is NOT supported

- Partitioning the MV can improve query performance and reduce costs


LIMITATIONS

- Each base table can be referenced by up to 100 materialized views from the same project, and 500 materialized views from the entire organization.

- When you add a description to a materialized view, the text can be at most 16,384 characters.

- A materialized view refresh job can run for up to 12 hours before it fails.

- The data of a materialized view cannot be updated or manipulated directly using operations such as COPY, EXPORT, LOAD, WRITE, or data manipulation language (DML) statements.

- You cannot replace an existing materialized view with a materialized view of the same name.

- The view SQL cannot be updated after the materialized view is created.

- A materialized view must reside in the same organization as its base tables, or in the same project if the project does not belong to an organization.

- Materialized views use a restricted SQL syntax and a limited set of aggregation functions. For more information, see Supported materialized views.

- Materialized views cannot be nested on other materialized views.

- Materialized views cannot query external tables, wildcard tables, other logical views, or snapshots.

- Only the GoogleSQL dialect is supported for materialized views.

- You can set descriptions for materialized views, but you cannot set descriptions for the individual columns in the materialized view.

- If you delete a base table without first deleting the materialized view, queries and refreshes of the materialized view fail. If you recreate the base table, you must also recreate the materialized view.

- If a materialized view has a change data capture-enabled base table, then that table can't be referenced in the same query as the materialized view.

Over BigLake tables

- Partitioning of the materialized view is not supported. The base tables can use hive partitioning but the materialized view storage cannot be partitioned in BigLake tables. This means that any deletion in a base table causes a full refresh of the materialized view.

- Joins between BigQuery managed tables and BigLake tables are not supported in a single materialized view definition.

- BigQuery BI Engine doesn't support acceleration of materialized views over BigLake tables.


BENIFITS

- Materialized views can optimize queries with high computation cost and small dataset results. 

- Processes that benefit from materialized views include online analytical processing (OLAP) operations that require significant processing with predictable and repeated queries like those in from extract, transform, load (ETL) processes or business intelligence (BI) pipelines.

- Aggregation of streaming data.

- Run queries that only read a particular subset of the table.

- Query joins, especially between large and small tables.

- Run queries that would benefit from a clustering scheme that differs from the base tables.


CRUD OPERATIONS

IAM permission: bigquery.tables.create Views are treated as table resources in BigQuery, in standard Views, you need access to tables as well, in Authorized views, access to views is enough.

To create a view for data that you don't own, you must have bigquery.tables.getData permission for that table.

Window Functions.description:
Window Functions


Window functions in BigQuery are a powerful way to perform calculations across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. Unlike aggregate functions (like SUM or AVG), which collapse rows into a single result, window functions allow you to keep your individual row detail while appending a calculated value. Here I am documenting all the functions available in Bigquery.

1. Ranking Functions:

  • ROW_NUMBER() - Unique sequential numbers
  • RANK() - Same rank for ties, gaps after
  • DENSE_RANK() - Same rank for ties, no gaps
  • NTILE() - Divide into buckets

2. Offset Functions:

  • LAG() - Access previous rows
  • LEAD() - Access next rows

3. Value Functions:

  • FIRST_VALUE() - First value in window
  • LAST_VALUE() - Last value in window
  • NTH_VALUE() - Nth value in window

4. Aggregate Functions:

  • SUM(), AVG(), COUNT(), MIN(), MAX() - As window functions

5. Distribution Functions:

  • PERCENT_RANK() - Relative rank as percentage
  • CUME_DIST() - Cumulative distribution
  • PERCENTILE_CONT() - Continuous percentile
  • PERCENTILE_DISC() - Discrete percentile

6. Window Frames:

  • ROWS - Physical row-based windows
  • RANGE - Logical value-based windows


Sample Data:

-- Our sample employee sales data
CREATE TEMP TABLE employee_sales AS
SELECT * FROM UNNEST([
  STRUCT('Alice' AS name, 'Sales' AS department, 5000 AS salary, 100 AS sales_amount, DATE('2024-01-15') AS sale_date),
  ('Bob', 'Sales', 6000, 150, DATE('2024-01-20')),
  ('Charlie', 'Engineering', 8000, NULL, DATE('2024-01-15')),
  ('Diana', 'Sales', 5500, 120, DATE('2024-02-10')),
  ('Eve', 'Engineering', 9000, NULL, DATE('2024-02-15')),
  ('Frank', 'Sales', 5200, 90, DATE('2024-02-20')),
  ('Grace', 'Engineering', 7500, NULL, DATE('2024-01-25')),
  ('Henry', 'Marketing', 6500, 80, DATE('2024-01-30')),
  ('Ivy', 'Marketing', 7000, 110, DATE('2024-02-05')),
  ('Jack', 'Marketing', 6800, 95, DATE('2024-02-12'))
]);


1. ROW_NUMBER():

Assigns a unique sequential integer to each row within a partition. Even if there are ties in the ORDER BY clause, each row gets a unique number.

#SYNTAX
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_num
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY department, row_num;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+---------+
| name    | department  | salary| row_num |
+---------+-------------+-------+---------+
| Eve     | Engineering | 9000  | 1       |
| Charlie | Engineering | 8000  | 2       |
| Grace   | Engineering | 7500  | 3       |
| Ivy     | Marketing   | 7000  | 1       |
| Jack    | Marketing   | 6800  | 2       |
| Henry   | Marketing   | 6500  | 3       |
| Bob     | Sales       | 6000  | 1       |
| Diana   | Sales       | 5500  | 2       |
| Frank   | Sales       | 5200  | 3       |
| Alice   | Sales       | 5000  | 4       |
+---------+-------------+-------+---------+


2. RANK()

Assigns a rank to each row within a partition. If there are ties, they receive the same rank, and the next rank will have a gap.

#SYNTAX
RANK() OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY rank;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+------+
| name    | department  | salary| rank |
+---------+-------------+-------+------+
| Eve     | Engineering | 9000  | 1    |
| Charlie | Engineering | 8000  | 2    |
| Grace   | Engineering | 7500  | 3    |
| Ivy     | Marketing   | 7000  | 4    |
| Jack    | Marketing   | 6800  | 5    |
| Henry   | Marketing   | 6500  | 6    |
| Bob     | Sales       | 6000  | 7    |
| Diana   | Sales       | 5500  | 8    |
| Frank   | Sales       | 5200  | 9    |
| Alice   | Sales       | 5000  | 10   |
+---------+-------------+-------+------+


3. DENSE_RANK()

Similar to RANK(), but without gaps in ranking when there are ties.

#SYNTAX
DENSE_RANK() OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY dense_rank;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+------------+
| name    | department  | salary| dense_rank |
+---------+-------------+-------+------------+
| Eve     | Engineering | 9000  | 1          |
| Charlie | Engineering | 8000  | 2          |
| Grace   | Engineering | 7500  | 3          |
| Ivy     | Marketing   | 7000  | 4          |
| Jack    | Marketing   | 6800  | 5          |
| Henry   | Marketing   | 6500  | 6          |
| Bob     | Sales       | 6000  | 7          |
| Diana   | Sales       | 5500  | 8          |
| Frank   | Sales       | 5200  | 9          |
| Alice   | Sales       | 5000  | 10         |
+---------+-------------+-------+------------+


4. NTILE()

Divides the ordered rows in a partition into a specified number of approximately equal groups or buckets.

#SYNTAX
NTILE(num_buckets) OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS bucket
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY salary DESC;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+--------+
| name    | department  | salary| bucket |
+---------+-------------+-------+--------+
| Eve     | Engineering | 9000  | 1      |
| Charlie | Engineering | 8000  | 1      |
| Grace   | Engineering | 7500  | 1      |
| Ivy     | Marketing   | 7000  | 1      |
| Jack    | Marketing   | 6800  | 2      |
| Henry   | Marketing   | 6500  | 2      |
| Bob     | Sales       | 6000  | 2      |
| Diana   | Sales       | 5500  | 3      |
| Frank   | Sales       | 5200  | 3      |
| Alice   | Sales       | 5000  | 3      |
+---------+-------------+-------+--------+


5. LAG()

Accesses data from a previous row in the result set without using a self-join.

#SYNTAX
LAG(expression, [offset], [default_value]) OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  LAG(salary, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary) AS prev_salary,
  salary - LAG(salary, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary) AS salary_diff
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY department, salary;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+-------------+
| name    | department  | salary| prev_salary | salary_diff |
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+-------------+
| Grace   | Engineering | 7500  | 0           | 7500        |
| Charlie | Engineering | 8000  | 7500        | 500         |
| Eve     | Engineering | 9000  | 8000        | 1000        |
| Henry   | Marketing   | 6500  | 0           | 6500        |
| Jack    | Marketing   | 6800  | 6500        | 300         |
| Ivy     | Marketing   | 7000  | 6800        | 200         |
| Alice   | Sales       | 5000  | 0           | 5000        |
| Frank   | Sales       | 5200  | 5000        | 200         |
| Diana   | Sales       | 5500  | 5200        | 300         |
| Bob     | Sales       | 6000  | 5500        | 500         |
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+-------------+


6. LEAD()

Accesses data from a subsequent row in the result set without using a self-join.

#SYNTAX
LEAD(expression, [offset], [default_value]) OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  LEAD(salary, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary) AS next_salary
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY department, salary;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+
| name    | department  | salary| next_salary |
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+
| Grace   | Engineering | 7500  | 8000        |
| Charlie | Engineering | 8000  | 9000        |
| Eve     | Engineering | 9000  | 0           |
| Henry   | Marketing   | 6500  | 6800        |
| Jack    | Marketing   | 6800  | 7000        |
| Ivy     | Marketing   | 7000  | 0           |
| Alice   | Sales       | 5000  | 5200        |
| Frank   | Sales       | 5200  | 5500        |
| Diana   | Sales       | 5500  | 6000        |
| Bob     | Sales       | 6000  | 0           |
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+


7. FIRST_VALUE()

Returns the first value in an ordered set of values within a window partition.

#SYNTAX
FIRST_VALUE(expression) OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
  [window_frame_clause]
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS highest_paid
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY department, salary DESC;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+--------------+
| name    | department  | salary| highest_paid |
+---------+-------------+-------+--------------+
| Eve     | Engineering | 9000  | Eve          |
| Charlie | Engineering | 8000  | Eve          |
| Grace   | Engineering | 7500  | Eve          |
| Ivy     | Marketing   | 7000  | Ivy          |
| Jack    | Marketing   | 6800  | Ivy          |
| Henry   | Marketing   | 6500  | Ivy          |
| Bob     | Sales       | 6000  | Bob          |
| Diana   | Sales       | 5500  | Bob          |
| Frank   | Sales       | 5200  | Bob          |
| Alice   | Sales       | 5000  | Bob          |
+---------+-------------+-------+--------------+


8. LAST_VALUE()

Returns the last value in an ordered set of values within a window partition.

#SYNTAX
LAST_VALUE(expression) OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
  ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department 
    ORDER BY salary DESC 
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS lowest_paid
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY department, salary DESC;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+
| name    | department  | salary| lowest_paid |
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+
| Eve     | Engineering | 9000  | Grace       |
| Charlie | Engineering | 8000  | Grace       |
| Grace   | Engineering | 7500  | Grace       |
| Ivy     | Marketing   | 7000  | Henry       |
| Jack    | Marketing   | 6800  | Henry       |
| Henry   | Marketing   | 6500  | Henry       |
| Bob     | Sales       | 6000  | Alice       |
| Diana   | Sales       | 5500  | Alice       |
| Frank   | Sales       | 5200  | Alice       |
| Alice   | Sales       | 5000  | Alice       |
+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+


9. NTH_VALUE()

Returns the value at a specific position (Nth row) in an ordered set of values within a window partition.

#SYNTAX
NTH_VALUE(expression, n) OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
  ORDER BY sort_expression
  ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
)


#EXAMPLE
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  NTH_VALUE(name, 2) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department 
    ORDER BY salary DESC 
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS second_highest_paid
FROM employee_sales
ORDER BY department, salary DESC;


#OUTPUT
+---------+-------------+-------+---------------------+
