GCP - BigQuery.description:
BigQuery

BigQuery is Google Cloud's fully managed, serverless data warehouse designed for large-scale data analytics. 


Architecture:

BigQuery uses a unique architecture that separates compute and storage, which is fundamental to its performance and scalability.


1. Colossus: The Storage Layer

Colossus is Googleâ€™s latest generation distributed file system and successor to the original Google File System (GFS).

  • Columnar Format (Capacitor): Data isn't stored in rows like a traditional spreadsheet. Instead, it uses a format called Capacitor. If you query 2 columns out of 100, Colossus only reads the files for those 2 columns.
  • Durability & Replication: When you save data, Colossus automatically shards it (splits it into chunks) and replicates it across multiple disks and zones. This ensures 11 nines (99.999999999%) of durability.
  • Separation: Because storage is on Colossus and compute is elsewhere, you can store 10PB of data for years without paying for any "running" servers. You only pay for the bytes stored.


2. Dremel: The Compute Engine

Dremel is the execution engine that turns your SQL into a massive parallel operation. It uses a multi-level serving tree to execute queries.

  • Root Server: Receives the query, looks at the metadata, and breaks the query into smaller "pieces" (shards).
  • Mixers: These are intermediate nodes that aggregate results from the layer below.
  • Leaf Nodes (Slots): These are the workers. A "slot" is a unit of CPU and RAM. Thousands of slots can work on a single query simultaneously. They talk directly to Colossus to pull the specific data needed.


3. Jupiter: The Network Fabric

In most architectures, "moving data" is the bottleneck. Jupiter is Google's petabit-scale data center network.

  • It provides enough bandwidth ($1 \text{ Petabit/sec}$) to allow the Dremel slots to read data from Colossus as if the data were sitting on a local hard drive.
  • Without Jupiter, the separation of storage and compute would be too slow to be useful.


4. Borg: Custer Management System

BigQuery is a "serverless" data warehouse, Borg is the engine that actually manages the "servers" behind the scenes. While you never interact with Borg directly, it is the foundational layer that allows BigQuery to scale from a single user to thousands of concurrent queries across petabytes of data without you having to provision a single virtual machine.

1. Orchestrating "Slots"

When you run a SQL query, BigQuery calculates how much processing power is needed. This power is measured in slots (units of CPU and RAM).

  • Borgâ€™s Role: It is responsible for finding available hardware in Google's data centers and instantly spinning up these slots.
  • Scale: Borg can orchestrate thousands of machines for a single query in seconds and then release them as soon as the query is finished.


2. Running the Dremel Engine

Dremel is the actual software that executes your SQL. However, Dremel doesn't run on "nothing"â€”it runs as a job on Borg.

  • Borg assigns Dremel tasks to specific machines.
  • It ensures that if one machine fails during your query, the task is immediately moved to another healthy machine, making your query execution highly fault-tolerant.

3. Resource Sharing and Efficiency

Borg allows BigQuery to be a multi-tenant service. It manages a massive pool of hardware and "packs" jobs together to ensure that no CPU cycles are wasted. This is why BigQuery is often cheaper than maintaining your own cluster; Borg is constantly optimizing the hardware usage across all of Googleâ€™s services.


***Borg is actually the internal predecessor to Kubernetes.Many of the concepts you might know from Kubernetes (like pods, services, and labels) originated from the Borg system used to run BigQuery.


4. Metadata and Catalog:

BigQuery maintains extensive metadata about your tables, including statistics about data distribution, which helps the query optimizer make intelligent decisions about execution plans.

Implementations.description:
Python Implementation

Overview

When using Google Cloud Spanner in Airflow or Python applications, you interact with it through the Google Cloud Spanner Python Client Library.

Unlike traditional databases that maintain persistent connections (like TCP sockets), Spanner uses a Session-based model optimized for massive scale and distributed architecture.

Key Difference: Traditional databases keep one open connection per client. Spanner automatically manages a pool of sessions behind the scenes, optimizing for global distribution and high throughput.


1. The Python API Structure

Spanner follows a hierarchical object model: Client â†’ Instance â†’ Database â†’ Session

from google.cloud import spanner

# 1. Initialize Client (authenticates and connects to Spanner)
spanner_client = spanner.Client(project='my-project-id')

# 2. Get Instance reference (logical container for databases)
instance = spanner_client.instance('my-instance-id')

# 3. Get Database reference (where your tables live)
database = instance.database('my-database-id')

Important Notes:

  • The Client object is thread-safe and should be reused across your application
  • Creating a Client is expensive; create it once and reuse it
  • Instance and Database objects are lightweight references, not actual connections
  • Actual sessions are created automatically when you execute queries


2. Transactions in Spanner

Spanner provides External Consistency - the strongest form of ACID compliance globally. This means transactions across the world are serializable and globally ordered using TrueTime.

A. Read-Write Transactions

When to Use: When you need to read data and then modify it based on that read.

Behavior:

  • Uses Optimistic Concurrency Control (not pessimistic locking)
  • If another transaction modifies the data you're reading, Spanner automatically retries your transaction
  • Maximum 3 automatic retries by default
  • All reads and writes are buffered until commit

Best Practice: Always use database.run_in_transaction() - it handles retries automatically.

def transfer_money(transaction, from_user, to_user, amount):
    # Read current balances
    row = transaction.execute_sql(
        "SELECT Balance FROM Users WHERE UserId = @id",
        params={'id': from_user},
        param_types={'id': spanner.param_types.INT64}
    ).one()
    
    balance = row[0]
    
    if balance < amount:
        raise ValueError("Insufficient funds")
    
    # Update both accounts (DML)
    transaction.execute_update(
        "UPDATE Users SET Balance = Balance - @amount WHERE UserId = @id",
        params={'amount': amount, 'id': from_user},
        param_types={'amount': spanner.param_types.INT64, 'id': spanner.param_types.INT64}
    )
    
    transaction.execute_update(
        "UPDATE Users SET Balance = Balance + @amount WHERE UserId = @id",
        params={'amount': amount, 'id': to_user},
        param_types={'amount': spanner.param_types.INT64, 'id': spanner.param_types.INT64}
    )

# Execute transaction (handles retries automatically)
database.run_in_transaction(transfer_money, from_user=1, to_user=2, amount=100)

Key Points:

  • Everything inside the function must be idempotent (safe to retry)
  • Don't perform external API calls or non-idempotent operations inside transactions
  • Transaction limit: 20,000 mutations maximum

B. Read-Only Transactions

When to Use: For consistent reads across multiple queries without needing to modify data.

Behavior:

  • Provides a snapshot of the database at a specific timestamp
  • No locks acquired (very efficient)
  • Multiple queries see the exact same data state
  • Can specify exact timestamp or "strong read" (latest data)
# Snapshot read at a specific point in time
with database.snapshot() as snapshot:
    # All queries see data from the same timestamp
    users = snapshot.execute_sql("SELECT * FROM Users")
    orders = snapshot.execute_sql("SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE UserId = @id",
                                  params={'id': 1},
                                  param_types={'id': spanner.param_types.INT64})
    
    # Both queries guaranteed to be consistent with each other

Use Cases:

  • Generating reports that need consistency across multiple tables
  • Analytics queries
  • Data exports where consistency matters

C. Partitioned DML

When to Use: For bulk updates or deletes affecting millions of rows (e.g., data cleanup, archival).

Behavior:

  • Spanner splits the operation across multiple partitions automatically
  • Does not provide full ACID guarantees (eventually consistent)
  • No transaction size limits
  • Cannot read-your-own-writes within the same operation
  • Much faster for large-scale operations
# Delete old records (affects millions of rows)
row_count = database.execute_partitioned_dml(
    "DELETE FROM Logs WHERE Timestamp < @cutoff_date",
    params={'cutoff_date': '2024-01-01'},
    param_types={'cutoff_date': spanner.param_types.DATE}
)

print(f"Deleted {row_count} rows")

Key Differences from Regular DML:

  • No atomicity: If it fails midway, some rows are already deleted
  • Cannot be rolled back
  • Much higher throughput for large datasets
  • Use for maintenance operations, not user-facing transactions

3. The DML Way (Data Manipulation Language)

DML in Spanner uses standard SQL syntax (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) but must be executed within a transaction context.

Basic DML Example:

def update_user_balance(transaction, user_id, amount):
    # Execute DML statement
    dml_query = "UPDATE Users SET Balance = Balance + @amount WHERE UserId = @id"
    
    row_count = transaction.execute_update(
        dml_query,
        params={'amount': amount, 'id': user_id},
        param_types={
            'amount': spanner.param_types.INT64,
            'id': spanner.param_types.INT64
        }
    )
    
    return row_count  # Returns number of rows modified

# Execute the transaction
rows_updated = database.run_in_transaction(update_user_balance, user_id=1, amount=100)
print(f"Updated {rows_updated} rows")

DML Best Practices:

  1. Always use parameterized queries (never string formatting):
# WRONG - SQL Injection risk and no query plan caching
query = f"UPDATE Users SET Name = '{user_name}' WHERE UserId = {user_id}"

# CORRECT - Safe and allows Spanner to cache execution plan
query = "UPDATE Users SET Name = @name WHERE UserId = @id"
params = {'name': user_name, 'id': user_id}
param_types = {'name': spanner.param_types.STRING, 'id': spanner.param_types.INT64}
  1. Batch multiple DML statements in one transaction:
def batch_updates(transaction):
    # Multiple DML operations in one transaction
    transaction.execute_update("UPDATE Users SET Active = true WHERE UserId = 1")
    transaction.execute_update("INSERT INTO AuditLog (Action, Timestamp) VALUES ('user_activated', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())")
    transaction.execute_update("DELETE FROM PendingActions WHERE UserId = 1")

database.run_in_transaction(batch_updates)
  1. Check affected row counts for validation:
def conditional_update(transaction, user_id, expected_version):
    row_count = transaction.execute_update(
        "UPDATE Users SET Balance = Balance + 100, Version = Version + 1 WHERE UserId = @id AND Version = @version",
        params={'id': user_id, 'version': expected_version},
        param_types={'id': spanner.param_types.INT64, 'version': spanner.param_types.INT64}
    )
    
    if row_count == 0:
        raise ValueError("Optimistic lock failed - record was modified by another transaction")

database.run_in_transaction(conditional_update, user_id=1, expected_version=5)

4. Mutations vs DML: Detailed Comparison

Spanner offers two ways to modify data. Choose based on your use case:

FeatureDML (SQL)MutationsSyntaxINSERT INTO..., UPDATE..., DELETE...database.insert(), database.update(), database.delete()Read-Your-Writesâœ… Yes - Can read changes immediately in same transactionâŒ No - Changes buffered and applied at commitConditional Logicâœ… Yes - WHERE Balance > 100âŒ No - Blind writes onlyComputed Valuesâœ… Yes - SET Balance = Balance + 10âŒ No - Must compute in applicationPerformanceSlower for simple inserts (query parsing overhead)âš¡ Faster for bulk inserts (no parsing)Ease of UseFamiliar for SQL developersMore verbose, programmaticBest ForLogic-heavy updates, conditional operationsHigh-throughput blind writesTransaction Limit20,000 mutations per transaction20,000 mutations per transaction

When to Use DML:

# Use DML when logic depends on current values
def increment_counter(transaction, counter_id):
    transaction.execute_update(
        "UPDATE Counters SET Count = Count + 1 WHERE CounterId = @id",
        params={'id': counter_id},
        param_types={'id': spanner.param_types.INT64}
    )

database.run_in_transaction(increment_counter, counter_id=1)

When to Use Mutations:

# Use Mutations for simple, high-throughput inserts
def bulk_insert_logs(transaction):
    transaction.insert(
        table='Logs',
        columns=['LogId', 'Message', 'Timestamp'],
        values=[
            (1, 'User logged in', '2024-01-01 10:00:00'),
            (2, 'User logged out', '2024-01-01 11:00:00'),
            (3, 'User updated profile', '2024-01-01 12:00:00')
        ]
    )

database.run_in_transaction(bulk_insert_logs)

5. Additional Critical Considerations

Session Management

Automatic vs Manual Sessions:

# Automatic (recommended) - library manages sessions
database.run_in_transaction(my_function)

# Manual (advanced use cases only)
with database.session() as session:
    with session.transaction() as transaction:
        # Your code here
        pass

Best Practice: Let the library manage sessions. Manual session management is only needed for advanced scenarios like long-running batch jobs.

Error Handling

Handling Aborted Transactions:

from google.api_core.exceptions import Aborted

try:
    database.run_in_transaction(my_function)
except Aborted:
    # Transaction was aborted due to conflicts
    # run_in_transaction already retried 3 times
    print("Transaction failed after retries")
except Exception as e:
    # Other errors (e.g., constraint violations)
    print(f"Error: {e}")

Performance Tips

  1. Avoid hotspots - Don't use sequential IDs as primary keys:
# BAD - Creates hotspot
CREATE TABLE Users (
    UserId INT64 NOT NULL,  -- Sequential IDs concentrate writes
    ...
) PRIMARY KEY (UserId)

# GOOD - Distributes writes evenly
import uuid
user_id = str(uuid.uuid4())  # Use UUIDs or hash-based keys
  1. Batch operations when possible:
# Instead of 100 separate transactions
for i in range(100):
    database.run_in_transaction(insert_one_row, i)

# Do one transaction with 100 inserts
def batch_insert(transaction):
    for i in range(100):
        transaction.insert('MyTable', columns=['Id', 'Value'], values=[i, f'value_{i}'])

database.run_in_transaction(batch_insert)
  1. Use appropriate transaction types - Don't use read-write when read-only suffices.

Connection Pooling

The Python client library automatically manages connection pooling. You can configure it:

from google.cloud.spanner_v1 import FixedSizePool

# Custom pool size (default is 10)
pool = FixedSizePool(size=25)
database = instance.database('my-database', pool=pool)

Summary Checklist

âœ… Use DML when:

  • Updates depend on existing values (Balance = Balance + 10)
  • You need conditional logic (WHERE clauses)
  • You need to read-your-own-writes in the same transaction

âœ… Use Mutations when:

  • Doing simple, high-throughput inserts
  • No conditional logic needed
  • Maximizing write performance

âœ… Use Transactions (run_in_transaction) to:

  • Ensure atomic "all-or-nothing" operations
  • Get automatic retry handling
  • Maintain data consistency

âœ… Use Parameterized Queries (@param) to:

  • Prevent SQL injection attacks
  • Allow Spanner to cache query execution plans
  • Improve performance and security

âœ… Use Partitioned DML for:

  • Bulk deletes or updates affecting millions of rows
  • Maintenance operations (data cleanup, archival)
  • When eventual consistency is acceptable

âœ… Use Read-Only Transactions for:

  • Consistent multi-query reads
  • Reports and analytics
  • When you don't need to modify data

GCP - Cloud Spanner.description:
Google Cloud Spanner

relational databases: are great for consistency but hard to scale

non-relational databases: scales easily but loses consistency.

Spaner: is the first database to provide both

Along side this spanner also:

1. Fully Managed

This means Google handles the "heavy lifting" of the infrastructure. You don't have to worry about:

  • Sharding: Manually breaking your data into pieces to fit on multiple servers. Spanner does this automatically.
  • Maintenance: Patching, hardware failures, and backups are handled by Google without downtime.
  • Replication: You just tell Spanner which regions you want your data in, and it handles the copying and synchronization.


2. Mission-Critical

In tech, "mission-critical" refers to systems that must never fail. Spanner is designed for 99.999% (five 9s) availability.

  • The "Five 9s": This equates to less than 5 minutes of downtime per year.
  • High Availability: It uses synchronous replication, meaning if a whole data center goes offline, your database stays up and your data remains safe.


3. Transactional Consistency

This is the "magic" of Spanner. In many distributed databases, if you update data in New York, someone in London might see the old data for a few seconds (this is called "eventual consistency").

  • Strong Consistency: Spanner guarantees that once a transaction is committed, everyone in the world sees the new data immediately.
  • ACID Compliance: It ensures transactions are Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, and Durableâ€”essential for things like banking or inventory where "double-spending" or "selling the last item twice" would be a disaster.


4. Global Scale

Most databases are limited to one "master" server for writes. Spanner can scale horizontally across thousands of servers and across multiple continents.

  • TrueTime API: To keep everything consistent globally, Spanner uses specialised hardware (atomic clocks and GPS antennas) in Googleâ€™s data centers to synchronize time with nanosecond precision. This allows it to order transactions correctly even if they happen on opposite sides of the planet.

TrueTime API: Simple Explanation

What is TrueTime?

TrueTime is Google's specially designed clock system that provides accurate time across all data centers worldwide. It's the core technology that makes Cloud Spanner's global consistency possible.

The Problem It Solves

Computer clocks naturally drift over time. A server in New York might show 10:00:05 while a server in London shows 10:00:03 due to clock skew. When processing transactions globally, this creates serious problems with data consistency.

How TrueTime Works?

Hardware Foundation

Google installed GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every data center. These provide highly accurate time references.

Time Intervals, Not Exact Time

TrueTime doesn't claim to know the exact time. Instead, it returns a time interval:

TrueTime.now() = [earliest possible time, latest possible time]
Example: [10:00:05.001, 10:00:05.007]

This means "the actual time is definitely somewhere in this 6-millisecond window."


The Commit Wait

When a transaction is ready to commit, Spanner:

1. Assigns it a timestamp

2. **Waits** until that timestamp is guaranteed to be in the past everywhere

3. Only then confirms the transaction as committed

This wait period is typically 5-7 milliseconds.


Why This Matters

Global Transaction Ordering

TrueTime ensures that if Transaction A finishes before Transaction B starts (in real time), then A's timestamp will always be earlier than B's timestamp. This is true even if they happen on opposite sides of the planet.

No Conflicting Writes

Traditional distributed databases can have newer data accidentally overwritten by older data due to clock differences. TrueTime eliminates this problem completely.


Real-World Example:

Scenario: Bank Account Transfer

You have $1000 in your bank account. Two transactions happen almost simultaneously:


Transaction 1 (New York): You withdraw $100 at an ATM

- Starts at TrueTime interval [10:00:05.001, 10:00:05.007]

- Spanner assigns timestamp: 10:00:05.007

- Waits 7 milliseconds to ensure this timestamp is in the past everywhere

- Commits: Balance = $900


Transaction 2 (Mumbai): Your friend deposits $200 to your account

- Starts at TrueTime interval [10:00:05.008, 10:00:05.014]

- Even though Mumbai's local server clock might be off, TrueTime knows the real time

- Spanner assigns timestamp: 10:00:05.014 (guaranteed to be after Transaction 1)

- Waits and commits: Balance = $1100


The Guarantee

Because of TrueTime:

- These transactions are processed in the correct order globally

- Your final balance is correct: $1000 - $100 + $200 = $1100

- No matter which data center you check from, you see the same result

- There's no possibility of the deposit being processed first and then overwritten by the withdrawal


Without TrueTime

Traditional systems might have:

- Mumbai server thinks its transaction happened at 10:00:05.005 (due to clock drift)

- New York thinks its transaction happened at 10:00:05.007

- Depending on which update arrives last, you might end up with wrong balance

- Different data centers might show different balances


The Trade-off

The 5-7 millisecond wait adds slight latency to every write operation. But in exchange, you get something unprecedented: absolute certainty that transactions are ordered correctly across the entire planet. This makes Spanner unique among distributed databases.


Spanner is a fully managed, mission-critical database service that brings together

  1. relational,
  2. graph,
  3. key-value, and
  4. search.

It offers transactional consistency at global scale, automatic, synchronous replication for high availability, and support for two SQL dialects: GoogleSQL (ANSI 2011 with extensions) and PostgreSQL.

Spanner editions

Spanner editions is a tier-based pricing model that provides different capabilities at different price points for various business and application needs:

  • Standard edition: provides a comprehensive suite of established capabilities that include all of the features that are Generally Available (GA) prior to September 24, 2024 along with selected additional capabilities, such as reverse ETL from BigQuery and scheduled backups, in single-region (regional) instance configurations.
  • Enterprise edition: builds on the Standard edition and offers multi-model capabilities including Spanner Graph, full-text search, and Vector Search. It also offers enhanced operational simplicity and data protection using managed autoscaling and incremental backups.
  • Enterprise Plus edition: designed for the most demanding workloads that require 99.999% availability with multi-region instance configurations and geo-partitioning support. This tier includes all Standard edition and Enterprise edition features.



Spanner Graph:

Spanner Graph is a native graph database built directly into the Cloud Spanner architecture. It allows you to model your data as Nodes and Edges while keeping all the Spanner benefits (all four points above).

Unlike other databases where you have to move data to a separate "Graph Database" (like Neo4j), Spanner Graph lets you treat your existing relational tables as a graph.


The Core Concepts: Nodes and Edges

In Spanner Graph, you don't just have "tables." You define a Property Graph schema:

  • Nodes (Vertices): Represent entities (e.g., Person, Account, Product). These are essentially rows in a table.
  • Edges (Relationships): Represent how nodes connect (e.g., Follows, Owns, Transfers). These are also stored as rows, but they specifically point from one node to another.
  • Properties: Both nodes and edges can have attributes (e.g., a Person has a name; a Transfers edge has an amount).

GCS Storage Classes

GCS has four main storage classes:

  1. Standard
  2. Nearline
  3. Coldline
  4. Archive

All classes have:

  • âœ… Same durability (11 Ã— 9s = 99.999999999%)
  • âœ… Same availability
  • âœ… Same API, tools, and security
  • âŒ Different cost and access characteristics

1. Standard Storage

Best For

  • Frequently accessed data
  • Real-time & active workloads

Use Cases

  • Data lakes
  • Web content
  • BigQuery external tables
  • Streaming ingestion data

Characteristics

  • High availability
  • No minimum storage duration
  • Lowest access latency
  • Higher storage cost, no retrieval fee

Example

User uploads, logs, images used daily



2. Nearline Storage

Best For

  • Data accessed less than once per month

Use Cases

  • Monthly reports
  • ETL intermediate backups
  • Data retained for compliance

Characteristics

  • Lower storage cost than Standard
  • Small retrieval cost
  • Minimum storage duration: 30 days

Example

Monthly financial data exports


3. Coldline Storage

Best For

  • Data accessed once or twice per year

Use Cases

  • Disaster recovery
  • Long-term analytics archives
  • Compliance records

Characteristics

  • Much cheaper storage
  • Higher access cost
  • Minimum storage duration: 90 days

Example

Yearly logs kept for audits


4. Archive Storage

Best For

  • Rarely accessed data (long-term archival)

Use Cases

  • Legal records
  • Medical data
  • Regulatory backups

Characteristics

  • Lowest storage cost
  • Highest retrieval cost
  • Minimum storage duration: 365 days

Example

7-year compliance data
